verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.131.15 in the BORI critical edition; Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section CXXXIII (wisdomlib). Our id 5.133.17 matches neither BORI chapter nor verse; it follows another edition's numbering.
attribution_note: Nested narration: Vaishampayana to Janamejaya; Kunti tells the old story to Krishna to pass on to Yudhishthira; inside it Vidula speaks to her son Sanjaya. The BORI text spells the queen Vidura (vidurā); Ganguli and the vulgate have Vidula.
translation_note: BORI reads the plural (the wise do not grieve). "na prāṇānāṃ dhanāyate" means he does not cling to or treasure his own life; in context that is a warrior's readiness to risk death. Our "does not hoard his own life" is literal but obscure; the line rightly drops it.
context: Before the war Kunti sends Yudhishthira the story of the Kshatriya queen Vidula, who found her son lying dejected after the king of Sindhu defeated him. This verse sits inside her opening tirade: she tells him to blaze up for a moment rather than smoulder, says the sensible do not keep lamenting, and then demands that he either show his valour or meet death, asking what he is living for.

key_terms.sense: whether he has won the thing or not
the wise person does not keep lamenting
he takes up what comes next, without a gap
he does not hoard his life like treasure, i.e. does not let fear for his safety hold him back

core_teaching: Once a result is in, success or failure, the wise do not sit in lament; they move straight to the next necessary act and do not let fear for themselves hold them back.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Udyoga sec. CXXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as the sensible person not grieving over gain or loss but doing what must be done next, careless even of his life. It falls in a scathing speech urging prowess or a warrior's death.
The constituted text has the plural "the wise do not grieve". The verses after it tell the son to show valour or go to the certain end, and twice ask him what he lives for.

practical_reading: Used against rumination after a setback: let the result register, then find the very next concrete step and take it, instead of waiting for the sting to fade before acting again.
misreadings: Not a call to be careless with one's life or health: the phrase about not hoarding life is a warrior's readiness to risk battle.
Not "never feel grief": the target is prolonged lament that blocks action.
cautions: The surrounding speech is shaming and martial: Vidula calls her son a eunuch and asks what he is alive for. Never pair with a reader who sounds hopeless or mentions not wanting to live.
Keep "does not hoard his life" out of any reading for someone in distress; it can read as indifference to living.
speaks_to: someone replaying a failure (exam, rejection, lost deal) who needs to restart
a person who has just got a result, good or bad, and is drifting
athletes, founders, job-seekers after a loss
not_for: bereavement
depression or suicidal thoughts
someone being pushed by family into dangerous risks
research_note: No classical commentary (Nilakantha) was available online; notes rest on Ganguli and the BORI text.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.131.18ef-19ab (BORI); Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section CXXXIII (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Vidula to her son Sanjaya, inside Kunti's story told to Krishna for Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit has two typos: आजानेयकतं should be आजानेयकृतं (ājāneya-kṛtam, "what a thoroughbred does"), and सत्वं should be सत्त्वं. The translation is sound; Ganguli likewise has well-bred horses straining under heavy loads as the model.
context: Still in Vidula's first speech. Just before, she says a sinking man should drag the enemy down with him and that even someone cut off at the roots must not despair. Just after, she tells him to raise up the family line that sank because of him. Her son has not yet answered.

key_terms.sense: lifting the yoke, he should pull it forward
a thoroughbred, a horse of good breeding that keeps pulling
one's own power of effort and agency

core_teaching: Even when everything seems cut away, take up your burden again as a good horse leans into a heavy load; rouse your strength and self-respect and recognise the capacity for effort that is yours.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Udyoga sec. CXXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: horses of mettle put out all their strength for heavy loads; remembering them, gather strength and honour and know what your manhood consists in. Raise the family that sank through you.
The verse straddles 18ef-19ab; the preceding half-verse says that even one whose roots are cut must never despair. The reading is ājāneyakṛtaṃ, "the deed of a thoroughbred".

practical_reading: A call to pick up an abandoned responsibility after a defeat: remember what steady, well-trained effort looks like and act from self-respect rather than from shame.
misreadings: Pauruṣa here means effort and agency, not machismo; the gendered insults around it are not the teaching.
Not "push through no matter what": a thoroughbred pulls well because it is trained and cared for.
cautions: The surrounding speech shames the son in gendered terms ("neither man nor woman"); a reading should borrow the courage, not the tone.
speaks_to: someone who has dropped a duty after a setback
rebuilding a business or career after failure
a student going back to study after failing
someone who needs to remember their own capacity
not_for: burnout or exhaustion where rest is the need
someone whose self-worth is already under attack at home

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.133.22-23ab (BORI); Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section CXXXV (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Vidula (the mother) to her son, after he asks her for a method; inside Kunti's story.
translation_note: BORI reads putrātmā nāvamantavyaḥ ("son, the self must not be despised"), same sense. "pūrvābhir asamṛddhibhiḥ" is "because of earlier failures"; Ganguli takes it loosely as "by anticipations of failure". Our translation is accurate.
context: The son finally pushes back: her heart is steel, and with no treasury or allies how can he win? Then he asks her for a way and promises to follow it. Her tone changes from scorn to counsel. This is her first piece of advice; she goes on to say results are uncertain but effort is the only route, and then gives a plan to win over the enemy's disaffected.

key_terms.sense: do not belittle or despise yourself
fortunes that were not, come to be

core_teaching: Past failures are no reason to think less of yourself, because fortunes come and go; but a fresh start should be made with judgment, not from wounded resentment.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Udyoga sec. CXXXV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's mother tells her son not to disgrace himself by expecting failure: what was not gained has been gained, what was gained has been lost, and goals should never be pursued in anger and folly.
The constituted text heads this "the mother said". It answers the son's question about how to win without treasury or allies, so it is counsel given on request, no longer rebuke.

practical_reading: Separate the failure from the self: a bad run is a fact about circumstances, not a verdict on worth. Then check the motive for the comeback; restarting out of anger or to prove someone wrong tends to go badly.
misreadings: Not a promise that fortune will return; it says fortunes change, both ways.
Not permission for a revenge project; the second half warns against exactly that.
cautions: Vidula's follow-up plan is wartime statecraft (recruiting the enemy's angry and humiliated). Keep the reading at the level of self-respect and wise beginnings.
speaks_to: someone who has turned a failure into an identity ("I am a failure")
restarting after bankruptcy, divorce, a failed exam or a layoff
someone tempted to act out of resentment
not_for: acute bereavement (the verse is about fortunes, not people)
someone whose loss came from another's abuse, who may hear it as "move on"

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.133.23cd-25ab (BORI); Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section CXXXV (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Vidula to her son, inside Kunti's story.
translation_note: Accurate. The final half-verse (aikaguṇyam anīhāyām...) says non-effort has a single outcome, absence of result; our last sentence carries it. Ganguli: without exertion only one result, failure; with exertion, two.
context: Directly continues the previous verse. After saying fortunes come and go, Vidula argues that uncertainty is no excuse: effort gives two possible outcomes, idleness only one. The next verses warn that whoever decides in advance that everything is uncertain shuts himself off from success, and urge him to act in the conviction that it will succeed.

key_terms.sense: the fruit of every action is always uncertain
some do not prosper, some do
the result is nothing at all

core_teaching: Every outcome is uncertain, so uncertainty cannot justify not trying: action gives two possibilities, success or not; inaction gives only one, nothing.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Udyoga sec. CXXXV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: success is always uncertain, yet people act and sometimes succeed; those who abstain never do. Whoever settles beforehand that results are uncertain makes success unreachable; cast off sloth and act believing it will happen.
The constituted text spells out both halves: inaction has one outcome, effort has two (fruit or no fruit), and knowing impermanence in advance should not be used to push away growth.

practical_reading: A reply to fear of failure and procrastination: you cannot remove uncertainty, but you can choose between a chance and a certainty of nothing. Apply, launch, ask, start.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that effort pays off; it explicitly allows that some who try do not succeed.
Not a judgment on people who tried and failed.
cautions: Spoken to rouse a reluctant prince to war; for someone who tried hard and lost, it can sound like blame.
speaks_to: someone hesitating to apply, launch, or ask
not_for: grief
someone exhausted after repeated effort who needs rest or comfort
someone whose failure was outside their control

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.7.13-14 (BORI, same numbering); Ganguli, Santi Parva section VII (wisdomlib). The same first line recurs at BORI 12.146.13.
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Arjuna, in his lament after the war.
translation_note: Minor: the disciplines (austerity, celibacy, worship, forbearance; fasts, sacrifices, vows, auspicious rites) are what parents undertake to obtain sons who will prosper; Ganguli has sires wishing for sons endowed with prosperity. The next lines show the hope includes the sons' support of the parents, so the line's "hoping only for their children's good" overstates the selflessness. "Sutān" is sons.
context: Right after the war Yudhishthira mourns Karna and all the slain. He describes how parents strive and pray for sons, carry them anxiously, and wonder whether they will live and grow strong; then he says those young men now lie dead and their parents' hopes are void. From this grief he argues for leaving the kingdom.

key_terms.sense: they long and strive for sons
vows, festive rites and auspicious ceremonies
they carry them for ten (lunar) months

core_teaching: Children are the object of long, costly hope: parents take on disciplines to have them and carry them with anxious expectation. In context the point is how much is lost when such children die.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. VII)
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli the verse opens a lament: parents ask whether their sons will survive and bring them joy, and now those youths are slain and the parents' expectations are fruitless.

The same first line returns at 12.146.13, where the sage Indrota rebukes King Janamejaya: parents strive for sons, yet his family's hopes in him came to nothing. Both uses stress hopes that can be dashed.

practical_reading: Can prompt gratitude for what parents invested before we were even born, and compassion for their worries; it also helps new parents name the weight of hope they carry.
misreadings: Not a claim that parents' love is purely selfless; the passage openly includes their hope of support.
Not a guilt lever ("look what your parents gave up").
cautions: In context this leads straight into the deaths of young sons and their parents' ruined hopes. Avoid for bereaved parents or anyone who has lost a child or a pregnancy.
Talks of conceiving and carrying children; can hurt readers facing infertility.
speaks_to: new or expecting parents reflecting on what they hope for
adult children making peace with what their parents gave
not_for: bereaved parents
infertility or pregnancy loss
estranged or abused children who would hear guilt
research_note: The library uses this as a verse on parental care; that is a fair extraction, but editors should know it is the first half of a lament for slain sons.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.7.34ab (BORI); the list of expiations is BORI star passage 8 (in some manuscripts only, not the constituted text). Ganguli, Santi Parva section VII (wisdomlib) includes the full list.
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Arjuna (vocative Dhanañjaya).
translation_note: The list has seven means: public declaration, remorse, giving, austerity, withdrawal or renunciation (nivṛtti), pilgrimage, and recitation of scripture; we keep four. "Upahanyate" is "is struck down, cancelled". The line's "give back" suggests restitution; the text says giving (dāna), i.e. charity.
context: Yudhishthira has called the war a sin. He says a sin can be cancelled by good acts and lists the means of expiation, then argues that renunciation is best, since the renouncer commits no new sins; so he will go to the forest. Arjuna immediately disputes this, praising wealth and kingship.
core_teaching: A wrong already done is not the end of the story: it can be outweighed by deliberate good action, beginning with owning it and feeling its weight.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. VII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli lists the means and adds that the renouncer is held incapable of new sin, which is why Yudhishthira decides to go to the woods and hand Arjuna the kingdom.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition (textual note, 12.7.34 and star passage 8)
commentaries.gist: Only the first line is in the constituted text; the itemised list of expiations is a manuscript addition, matching the brackets in our Sanskrit.

practical_reading: For someone stuck in guilt: name the wrong honestly, let the regret be real, then do concrete good, ideally repairing harm where possible, rather than either denying it or drowning in it.
misreadings: Not "good deeds cancel the need to apologise or repair harm to the person hurt".
Not Yudhishthira's conclusion that one should abandon one's duties; the epic rejects that.
cautions: Uses the language of sin (pāpa); a scrupulous or depressed reader may hear accusation. Lead with the hope, not the sin.
Spoken by a man in acute guilt-driven grief who is about to be argued out of his plan.
speaks_to: guilt over a past wrong and wanting a way forward
not_for: someone who was harmed and is told to absorb it
obsessive guilt spirals
readers wanting to buy off a wrong with charity
research_note: A close parallel list of expiations appears in the Manusmriti; not checked against a source here.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.17.3 (BORI, same numbering); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XVII (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Bhima.
translation_note: Accurate. BORI reads udaram evaikaṃ ("just one stomach"), same sense.
context: Bhima has urged Yudhishthira to stop grieving and enjoy the kingdom they won. Yudhishthira answers that discontent, attachment and pride drive Bhima's love of rule: even the sole ruler of the earth has one stomach, desire can never be filled, so conquer the stomach first. In the same speech he quotes Janaka's saying that nothing of his burns if Mithila burns.

key_terms.sense: one stomach, one person's real need

core_teaching: Owning more than one can use adds nothing to what one person actually needs; so praising accumulation and power for their own sake is misplaced.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the peerless monarch of the whole earth will have but one stomach, so why applaud this life? Desire is like fire fed with fuel; subdue the stomach with little food and conquer it first.
Same chapter and numbering. The speech goes on (12.17.17-18) to quote Janaka's verse about Mithila burning, linking this verse to the renunciation sayings elsewhere in the Shanti Parva.

practical_reading: A check on status-chasing: ask what you will actually use or enjoy, and notice how much striving serves appetite rather than need.
misreadings: Not a rule against earning, providing or leading; Yudhishthira is answered by his family and does take up the rule.
Not advice to under-eat.
cautions: The next lines in Ganguli praise subduing hunger with little food; avoid for readers with disordered eating.
Spoken by a grieving man arguing against his duties; the epic does not endorse his conclusion.
speaks_to: someone burnt out from chasing more
not_for: people in poverty or food insecurity
eating disorders
someone deciding to abandon responsibilities

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.17.4 (BORI, same numbering); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XVII (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Bhima.
translation_note: Accurate (BORI reads śakyā na māsena nararṣabha, same sense). The verse is descriptive; the line's "Stop trying to fill it" adds an imperative that is implied, not stated.
context: Continues the previous verse: after "one stomach", Yudhishthira says desire cannot be filled in a day, in months, or in a lifetime, and compares it to fire that grows when fed and dies down when not.
core_teaching: Desire is structurally unfillable: feeding it does not satisfy it, so a whole life spent filling it never arrives at enough.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: desires cannot be filled in a day or many months, not in a whole lifetime; fire fed with fuel blazes, unfed it goes out.
Constituted text has the same thought with minor wording differences; the "unfillable desire" idea recurs in Yayati's sayings and in Manki's song later in the Shanti Parva.

practical_reading: Notice the pattern of "one more" (purchase, promotion, follower count) and test whether feeding it ever produced lasting satisfaction; practise contentment as a skill.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all wanting; it is about craving as a bottomless hunger.
cautions: Same context as 12.17.3: grief-driven argument against duty; the fire-and-food image continues into fasting advice.
speaks_to: compulsive buying, scrolling or achievement treadmills
someone who "has everything" and is still restless
not_for: someone whose basic needs are unmet
eating disorders

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.26.31 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXV (wisdomlib). Our chapter number 25 is one lower than BORI.
attribution_note: Speaker is Vyasa, not Senajit. In BORI 12.26.29 Vyasa closes the quotation ("thus spoke the wise Senajit"); verses 30-31 are Vyasa's own summary. Ganguli agrees: the line "This is what Senajit said" comes before this verse. Listener Yudhishthira is correct.
translation_note: Our reading (paryāyataḥ sarvam avāpnuvanti, tasmān na muhyen na ca saṃprahṛṣyet) is a variant; BORI has "all these touch everyone here in turn, so the steady one should neither exult nor be resentful". Ganguli: neither elated nor depressed. Typo: अवाप्तुवन्ति should be अवाप्नुवन्ति.
context: Yudhishthira tells Vyasa no pleasure reaches him while widows lament. Vyasa replies that everything comes in its time, quotes the grieving King Senajit on how dwelling on loss feeds it, then adds this verse in his own voice and turns to telling Yudhishthira that battle, just rule and generous gifts are a king's sacrifice and yoga.

key_terms.sense: rise and fall, being and not-being
should be neither bewildered nor carried away

core_teaching: The pairs of opposites, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, life and death, visit everyone in rotation; seeing that, one keeps steady, neither crushed nor elated.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: after reporting Senajit, Vyasa says happiness and misery, prosperity and adversity, gain and loss, death and life wait on all creatures in turn, so the wise man of tranquil soul is neither elated nor depressed.
Senajit's song runs 12.26.14-28 and is closed at 26.29; this verse (26.31) belongs to Vyasa. Its BORI ending asks the steady person to neither exult nor be angry.

practical_reading: Used for equanimity in volatile seasons: when things go very well or very badly, remember the wheel turns for everyone and keep your footing.
misreadings: Not "feel nothing"; it targets being thrown off balance.
Not fatalism about injustice.
cautions: Lists death and life among the alternations; to someone freshly bereaved the call to stay unmoved can feel like being told not to mourn.
Vyasa's next move is to send Yudhishthira back to kingship and war-as-sacrifice.
speaks_to: someone riding a high or a low (markets, career, health swings)
a person comparing their bad season to others' good ones
not_for: fresh grief
someone suffering ongoing injustice
research_note: Fix speaker to Vyasa (to Yudhishthira); Senajit is quoted earlier in the same speech.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.27.28 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVII (wisdomlib). Our numbering is one chapter lower and one verse higher than BORI.
attribution_note: Vyasa to Yudhishthira (introduced by Vaishampayana). Setting is right: Yudhishthira has just declared he will fast to death.
translation_note: Accurate. Note that Ganguli reads saṃyoga/viprayoga as the coming together and dissolving of the constituents of beings, not only meeting and parting with people; both readings are possible.
context: Yudhishthira blames himself for Bhishma's fall and the deaths of the young and says he will sit and starve. Vyasa restrains him, tells him not to grieve beyond measure, and lists the certainties: unions end in separation, heaps in depletion, rises in falls, life in death. He ends by saying Yudhishthira was made for action and must not avoid it.

key_terms.sense: they come to be and cease to be

core_teaching: Coming together and coming apart are built into every born life, as bubbles form and vanish on water; seeing this is meant to limit excessive grief, not to forbid it.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXVII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Vyasa first says "this cannot be" to the fast, then that everything born meets dissolution like bubbles; everything risen falls, union ends in separation, life in death; and Yudhishthira was created for work.

The constituted text frames it as Vyasa forbidding a resolved fast unto death; his first line is "you should not grieve beyond measure". The next verse is the stock maxim that unions end in separation, life in death.

practical_reading: A way to hold impermanence gently: every relationship has a beginning and an end, which is a reason to cherish it now and to grieve without being destroyed.
misreadings: Not "relationships don't matter because they end".
Not "stop grieving"; Vyasa objects to grief beyond measure that turns into self-destruction.
cautions: The setting is a resolve to starve oneself to death. Any reading must not echo that setting for a reader who mentions not wanting to live; point to real help instead.
Impermanence talk can feel cold to fresh grief.
speaks_to: endings: moves, breakups, children leaving home, retirement
someone learning to hold relationships lightly and dearly
not_for: acute grief
suicidal thoughts
someone afraid of abandonment who may hear "everyone leaves"

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.28.40 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVIII (wisdomlib). Our chapter number is one lower than BORI.
attribution_note: Ashma to King Janaka, quoted by Vyasa to Yudhishthira (Vaishampayana narrating).
translation_note: BORI reads kvāsaṃ kvāsmi gamiṣyāmi ("where was I, where am I, where shall I go") and kam anuśoceyam ("for whom should I grieve"); our क्वासे looks corrupt. Ganguli matches our sense. The translation is faithful.
context: Vyasa, trying to lift Yudhishthira's grief, tells how the sage Ashma answered King Janaka, who asked how one should meet the arrival and loss of kin and wealth. Ashma describes how pleasure and pain take turns, how time carries everyone, and how family ties are like travellers meeting on a road; he ends by telling Janaka to live by scripture, honour ancestors and do his duties, and Janaka goes home free of grief. This verse follows the image of countless mothers, fathers, sons and wives met over many lives, and of family as a meeting on a road.

key_terms.sense: where was I, where will I go
why, and for whom, should I grieve
let one settle, make steady, the mind
a meeting on the road (Ashma's image for family ties)

core_teaching: In loss, step back and ask where you came from, where you are going and who you are; seeing life as a brief shared stretch of road steadies the mind.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: our union with wives, kin and friends is like travellers at a roadside inn; asking where am I, where shall I go, who am I, for whom do I grieve, one gains calm. Life turns like a wheel.
Verse 40ef adds that dwelling with dear ones is impermanent and samsara turns like a wheel; a manuscript line repeats that brother, mother, father and friend are a meeting on the road.

practical_reading: A contemplative prompt for later grief or life transitions: widen the frame beyond the immediate loss and ask what you are and what your journey is.
misreadings: Not "they were never really yours, so don't mourn".
Not a way to argue someone out of grief; the data's own misuse note is right.
cautions: Context assumes rebirth (countless parents and children over many lives); can feel dismissive to fresh grief.
The inn/road image for family can wound a newly bereaved spouse or parent.
speaks_to: someone overwhelmed who needs to step back
not_for: fresh bereavement, especially of a child or partner
someone feeling abandoned

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.28.48 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVIII (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Ashma to King Janaka, quoted by Vyasa.
translation_note: Our second half-line ("na punar vai samāgamaḥ", no reunion) is a variant not found in BORI or Ganguli. BORI: for all born beings neither fortnights nor nights come back; Ganguli likewise lists years, months, fortnights, days and nights. Our "do not meet again in the same way" adds words even to the variant. The line's "Be here for the ones in front of you" is an application, not in the verse. Suggest following BORI.
context: Vyasa, trying to lift Yudhishthira's grief, tells how the sage Ashma answered King Janaka, who asked how one should meet the arrival and loss of kin and wealth. Ashma describes how pleasure and pain take turns, how time carries everyone, and how family ties are like travellers meeting on a road; he ends by telling Janaka to live by scripture, honour ancestors and do his duties, and Janaka goes home free of grief. Here Ashma has just said that physicians fall ill, elixir-makers age, and ascetics and generous givers still meet old age and death.
core_teaching: Time spent does not come back for anyone born: days, months, years, nights are gone once gone. The point is to see time's one-way flow clearly and live accordingly.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: for all creatures born, years, months, fortnights, days and nights once passed never return; man is carried by Time, willing or not, onto the broad road all must walk.
The constituted text lists fortnights and nights in the second half-line, not "no reunion". The surrounding verses stress that medicine, elixirs, austerity and generosity do not stop aging and death.

practical_reading: Teachers use the line to sharpen priorities: time is the one resource that never refunds, so spend today on what and whom you value.
misreadings: Not a statement that the dead are lost forever (that comes only from the weak variant).
Not a reason for panic about time; Ashma uses it to steady the mind.
cautions: With our variant ("beings do not meet again") the verse is stark for anyone grieving; prefer the BORI reading.
Context dwells on illness and aging that medicine cannot stop.
speaks_to: someone deciding what matters this year
not_for: fresh grief
health anxiety
someone with a terminal diagnosis unless they ask for this frame
research_note: Data error: second half-line is a weakly attested variant; translation and line should be revised.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.28.51 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVIII (wisdomlib). The same idea recurs at BORI 12.307.9.
attribution_note: Ashma to King Janaka, quoted by Vyasa.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Vyasa, trying to lift Yudhishthira's grief, tells how the sage Ashma answered King Janaka, who asked how one should meet the arrival and loss of kin and wealth. Ashma describes how pleasure and pain take turns, how time carries everyone, and how family ties are like travellers meeting on a road; he ends by telling Janaka to live by scripture, honour ancestors and do his duties, and Janaka goes home free of grief. The verse follows the line that union with wife and kin is a meeting on the road, and precedes the question: where today are your father and grandfather? You do not see them, nor they you.

key_terms.sense: living together for ever, permanent companionship

core_teaching: Permanent companionship is not available to anyone, not even with one's own body; seeing this loosens the shock of separation.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: no one gains lasting companionship with anyone, not even with one's own body, so how with another? Then: where are your sire and grandsire now? Follow the scriptures and your duties.
Same wording in the constituted text; a near-identical line returns at 12.307.9 in a later consolation, showing it is a stock teaching of the Shanti Parva.

practical_reading: Used to hold people and health with open hands: every bond, including with our own body, is on loan, which is a reason for tenderness now.
misreadings: Not "don't get attached to anyone".
Not contempt for the body.
cautions: Next lines turn to dead fathers and grandfathers; mind readers recently bereaved of a parent.
Mentions parting from one's own body; handle with care for serious illness.
not_for: fresh bereavement
terminal illness unless the reader seeks this frame
health anxiety

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.29.13 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXIX (wisdomlib). Our chapter and verse are each one lower/higher than BORI.
attribution_note: Narada to King Srinjaya, recounted by Krishna to Yudhishthira at Arjuna's request.
translation_note: Our reading avimuktā mariṣyāmaḥ ("we shall die not freed") matches Ganguli; BORI reads avimuktaṃ cariṣyāmaḥ ("we shall go on not freed from joys and sorrows"). Translation fine. The line's "You're not alone in this" is a fair gloss.
context: Arjuna asks Krishna to comfort Yudhishthira. Krishna retells how Narada consoled King Srinjaya after his son died: this verse opens Narada's speech, followed by the lives of sixteen great kings, each said to surpass the boy and yet to have died, with the refrain that Srinjaya should not grieve. Srinjaya says his grief is gone and asks for his son; Narada restores him.

key_terms.sense: not released from joys and sorrows

core_teaching: Narada places one death inside the shared human condition: speaker, listener and all beings will die still tangled in joy and sorrow, so lament cannot set one apart.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXIX)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Narada says all of us, subject to happiness and misery, must die, so why sorrow, then recites ancient kings to dispel grief. Srinjaya, comforted, asks; Narada gives back his son Suvarnashthivin.

The Sixteen Kings episode is in the constituted text; its refrain tells Srinjaya not to grieve for a son lesser than those kings. The BORI reading of this verse speaks of living on, not dying, unfreed from joy and sorrow.

practical_reading: At its gentlest it says grief is shared, not a personal punishment: everyone, including those who comfort you, is in the same condition.
misreadings: Not "your loss is small because everyone dies".
Our misuse note says the story "is not telling a grieving parent to stop crying"; in fact its refrain does say "do not grieve". The verse should not be presented as validating tears either.
cautions: The son is miraculously restored at the end; a bereaved parent may find that painful.
The refrain compares the dead child unfavourably with legendary kings.
Speaks plainly of death to someone grieving a child.
not_for: bereaved parents in early grief
children
research_note: Misuse note in our data is partly inaccurate (see misreadings).

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.47.7 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section XLVIII on wisdomlib and mahabharataonline (our data says Ganguli XLVII; sacred-texts could not be checked and may number this stretch one lower).
attribution_note: Vaishampayana (narrator) to Janamejaya, answering his question about how Bhishma left his body.
translation_note: Accurate; Ganguli also has "pure heart". BORI reads prāñjaliḥ sthitaḥ ("stood with joined palms") for our prāñjaliḥ śuciḥ.
context: Janamejaya asks how Bhishma on the arrow-bed gave up his body and what yoga he held. Vaishampayana describes him, surrounded by sages, concentrating within, then turning in deed, mind and word to Krishna and singing the long hymn (Bhishma-stava-raja). Krishna, far away, perceives it, grants him knowledge, and sets out with the Pandavas to visit him.
core_teaching: Facing death in great pain, Bhishma gathers his whole being, act, thought and word, into one movement of attention toward Krishna.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: surrounded by sages like the moon among stars, Bhishma with pure heart and joined palms thought of Krishna in mind, word and act and praised him in a strong, cheerful voice.

The chapter is framed by Janamejaya's question about Bhishma's death; long lists of attending sages are manuscript additions. The hymn is placed here although Bhishma's teaching and death come later in the book.

practical_reading: A model for prayer or meditation in hard moments: bring body, mind and words to one point instead of letting pain scatter them.
misreadings: Not a claim that devotion removes pain; Bhishma is still on the arrows.
cautions: A deathbed scene with physical suffering; consider the reader's situation (illness, caregiving).
not_for: someone frightened of dying who did not ask for this
readers who reject devotional framing
research_note: Section number: wisdomlib and mahabharataonline both head the stava "Section XLVIII"; data says XLVII (perhaps sacred-texts numbering, not checkable here).

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.47.60 (BORI constituted text); repeated by Bhishma to Krishna at 12.51.8. Ganguli, Santi Parva section XLVIII (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Bhishma, in his hymn to Krishna.
translation_note: Accurate: Krishna's body is the colour of the (blue) flax flower and his garment yellow. Ganguli blurs this ("yellow robes of the colour of the Atasi flower") but footnotes atasi as flax.
context: Near the end of the hymn, after praising Krishna as the cosmic person and in his many forms, Bhishma says that those who bow to Govinda have no fear; manuscripts add that one bow to Krishna equals ten horse-sacrifices. The hymn closes with Bhishma's petition and a final salutation.

key_terms.sense: like the blue flax flower, dark-hued
the unfailing, the one who never slips

core_teaching: Bowing to Krishna, pictured in his familiar dark form and yellow garment, is offered as refuge from fear.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XLVIII, n. 18)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: those who worship Govinda of unfading prowess are freed from all fears; the next lines say one bow to Krishna equals ten horse-sacrifices and frees from rebirth. His note identifies atasi as flax.
The verse is in the constituted text, but the ten-horse-sacrifice lines between its halves are manuscript additions. Bhishma repeats the first line to Krishna's face at 12.51.8.

practical_reading: Used as a short prayer for anxious moments: picture the beloved form, bow inwardly, and let that be a place to stand.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will happen (our misuse note is right).
Not "fear means weak faith".
cautions: Spoken by a dying man; the hymn also contains rebirth and hell imagery nearby.
speaks_to: devotional readers seeking a short prayer
not_for: anxiety disorders where the reader may feel blamed for still being afraid
readers who reject devotional framing

verified_ref: Not in the BORI constituted text: BORI star passage 93 (lines 1-2), inserted after 12.47.60 in some manuscripts. Ganguli, Santi Parva section XLVIII (wisdomlib) includes it.
attribution_note: Bhishma, in his hymn to Krishna (manuscript addition).
translation_note: Accurate. BORI's apparatus reads -tara-kāṣṭha ("a log for crossing"); our -tari- ("boat") gives a similar sense. Nimnagā is a river; Ganguli has "ocean".
context: Part of a block of salutations that some manuscripts insert in the closing section of Bhishma's hymn, between "those who bow to Govinda have no fear" and his final petition.

key_terms.sense: whirlpools of the river of worldly existence
a log or plank to cross by

core_teaching: Vishnu is praised as protection against dread and as the one thing to hold onto when life's current spins you.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: salutations to the one who dispels fear of hell, a boat for those plunged in the eddies of worldly life; then to the friend of brahmins, cows and the world, Krishna and Govinda.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, star passage 93 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The editors relegated this salutation block to the apparatus as a manuscript addition; our brackets reflect that. It is devotional expansion, not the oldest layer.

practical_reading: An image for overwhelming periods: when life swirls, you do not need to swim out, only to hold on to something steady.
misreadings: Not fear-based religion; the stress is on rescue, not on hell.
cautions: Mentions hell; soften or drop that half for anxious readers.
Late devotional addition; present as part of the received hymn, not as Bhishma's oldest words.
not_for: readers with religious fear or scrupulosity
research_note: Not in the critical text; editors may want a flag.

verified_ref: Not in the BORI constituted text: BORI star passage 93 (lines 5-6), after 12.47.60. Ganguli, Santi Parva section XLVIII (wisdomlib) includes it.
attribution_note: Bhishma, in his hymn to Krishna (manuscript addition).
translation_note: Accurate. BORI's apparatus reads saṃsāra-ccheda ("cutting off saṃsāra"), our -uccheda, same sense. "Prāṇa-kāntāra" is the wilderness of life (of the life-breath).
context: Same inserted block as the preceding salutation, near the end of Bhishma's hymn; it is the classic statement of the power of the name Hari within the Mahabharata.

key_terms.sense: provisions for the wilderness-journey of life
medicine that cuts off worldly bondage

core_teaching: The name Hari is presented as food for the journey, medicine and rescue from grief: a portable refuge.

commentaries.who: Ganguli translation with note 19 (Santi sec. XLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli calls the two syllables the travelling stock for life's wilderness and the cure for worldly attachments; his note gives two readings of saṃsāra: attachments, or the round of rebirths ended by contemplation.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, star passage 93 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Relegated to the apparatus as a manuscript addition, as our brackets show; it reflects later name-devotion (nāma-māhātmya) layered onto the hymn.

practical_reading: A simple practice for hard days: repeat the name as provisions on a long road, a small, carryable source of steadiness.
misreadings: Not a cure that replaces medical, legal or emotional help (our misuse note is right).
Not magic words; in context it is the fruit of a lifetime's devotion.
cautions: Late devotional addition; present it as part of the recited hymn tradition.
speaks_to: devotional readers in grief or illness
someone wanting a simple daily practice
not_for: readers who might use prayer instead of treatment
non-devotional users
research_note: Not in the critical text.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.47.62 (BORI constituted text); repeated to Krishna at 12.51.9 (as tvatprapannāya). Ganguli, Santi Parva section XLVIII (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Bhishma to Krishna, in the hymn.
translation_note: Accurate. "Gatim iṣṭām" is the desired destination, in context the goal after death. Ganguli: seeking protection and devoted, desiring a happy end, he asks the lotus-eyed one to think of his good.
context: Bhishma's last petition in the hymn, after "may my sins perish as everything is full of Vishnu". He then bows saying "namah", and Krishna, perceiving his devotion, grants him divine knowledge. Bhishma repeats the same plea when Krishna stands before him (12.51.9).

key_terms.sense: the hoped-for destination, a good end
whatever is truly good (not merely pleasant)
please think of, keep in mind

core_teaching: Having done his part and taken refuge, Bhishma hands the choice of what is truly good for him to Krishna.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: I seek your protection and am devoted, desiring a happy end; lotus-eyed best of gods, think of what will be for my good. Bhishma then bows and Krishna grants him knowledge of past, present and future.
In the constituted text in both places: once in the hymn, once said face to face when Krishna arrives, right after Bhishma repeats the flax-flower verse.

practical_reading: A prayer of trust after effort: I have done what I could; let what is truly good, not just what I want, unfold.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop making choices (our misuse note is right).
Shreyas is the truly good, not guaranteed comfort.
cautions: A deathbed prayer for a good end; for ill or elderly readers it may land as "prepare to die".
speaks_to: letting go of control after doing one's part
not_for: someone avoiding a decision
readers frightened by mortality

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.52.11 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LII (wisdomlib). Our chapter number is one lower than BORI.
attribution_note: Bhishma to Krishna.
translation_note: Accurate. "Tiṣṭhāmi" is "I remain, I live on"; Ganguli: I am only barely alive through your energy.
context: Krishna has asked Bhishma to teach Yudhishthira. Bhishma protests that in Krishna's presence he cannot speak: his arrow-wounds burn, his mind is clouded, his breath is failing, he cannot tell the directions or sky from earth, and he lives only by Krishna's power, so Krishna should teach. Krishna then grants him freedom from pain, hunger and confusion and clear vision.

key_terms.sense: I cannot make out the directions
I stand, I hold on, I remain alive

core_teaching: In extreme pain and disorientation, Bhishma admits he has no footing of his own and is sustained only by the divine.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Bhishma says his mind is agitated by arrow pain, vitals burning, utterance failing; he cannot distinguish the compass points or sky from earth and is barely alive through Krishna's energy, so Krishna should speak.
Same wording in the constituted text; the verse belongs to Bhishma's refusal to teach, which Krishna answers with the boon that removes his pain.

practical_reading: Gives words to utter depletion: it is honest to say "I can't tell up from down; I am held up by something beyond me".
misreadings: Not passivity; the next scene has Bhishma teaching for days. (Our misuse note cites Gita 18.63, which is not from this context.)
cautions: Describes severe pain and dying; can be strongly validating or frightening for the seriously ill.
speaks_to: exhaustion, illness, burnout at its worst
devotional readers who feel they are holding on by grace
not_for: readers in crisis who need practical help first
non-devotional users

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.54.17 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LIV (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Bhishma to Krishna, the morning after the boon.
translation_note: Accurate for our reading (vārṣṇeya ... vyapagatāni me), which Ganguli follows ("O you of Vrishni's race"). BORI has govinda ... vyapagatānagha.
context: Next morning the Pandavas and Krishna return. Krishna asks whether Bhishma slept well and whether his mind is clear and free of pain. Bhishma answers with this verse and adds that past, present and future, all the Vedic and regional duties, and kingcraft are now clear to him, so he feels young and able to teach.
core_teaching: Bhishma testifies that by Krishna's grace his burning, fog, exhaustion and pain lifted at once, clearing him for his last work.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: burning, stupefaction, fatigue, exhaustion, illness and pain have left me in a single day; past, present and future are clear as a fruit in my hand.
Constituted text addresses Govinda; the relief is the fulfilment of the boon Krishna gave at 12.52. Bhishma still dies weeks later at the solstice.

practical_reading: For relief after a hard stretch: name what has eased and give thanks, without assuming the struggle is over.
misreadings: Not a promise of healing; keep up medical care (our misuse note is right).
Relief here is to enable service, not an escape from death.
cautions: Readers with chronic pain may feel their own lack of relief as lack of grace.
speaks_to: a fog lifting after depression (with care)
not_for: chronic or terminal illness without relief
readers who might stop treatment

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.54.23 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LIV (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Bhishma to Krishna.
translation_note: Accurate. BORI reads yuveva cāsmi saṃvṛttaḥ, same sense ("I have become as if young").
context: Same morning conversation. Having reported his relief and clarity, Bhishma says meditation on Krishna has made him feel young and able to speak the good; he then asks why Krishna does not teach Yudhishthira himself, and Krishna replies that he wants Bhishma's fame to grow.

key_terms.sense: strengthened by continual meditation on you
able to speak what is truly good

core_teaching: Remembrance of the divine renews even the old and wounded, making them able to give what is truly good to others.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: strengthened by meditation on Krishna, Bhishma feels young again and competent to discourse on what is beneficial, then asks why Krishna does not teach himself.
Same verse in the constituted text; Krishna's answer is that he steps back so Bhishma's words will be honoured as long as the world lasts.

practical_reading: For elders and mentors: inner renewal can come late in life, and its natural use is passing on what one knows.
misreadings: Not a promise of physical youth.
cautions: Bhishma is still dying; avoid suggesting the body will recover.
speaks_to: older readers taking on mentoring or teaching
renewal after a long illness or depression
someone asked to step up and teach
not_for: readers in active decline who may feel failure for not feeling renewed

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.56.16 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LVI (wisdomlib). Our chapter number is one lower than BORI.
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira, at the start of his teaching on kingship (rājadharma).
translation_note: First line exact. Our second line (ghaṭetaivaṃ sadātmānam, "let him always apply himself thus") is the vulgate reading, which Ganguli follows (redoubled exertion in the same act). BORI reads ghaṭate vinayas tāta ("discipline is what is fitting, my son"). The translation fits our Sanskrit.
context: Bhishma opens his instruction: a king should honour gods and brahmins, and always strive in exertion (utthāna), since fate does nothing without it; fate and effort go together, but effort is primary. Then this verse: do not burn with distress over a failed undertaking; apply yourself again. He moves on to truth as the king's chief means of success.

key_terms.sense: exertion, getting up and acting (the theme of the passage)
the highest policy, the best rule

core_teaching: A failed undertaking is not a reason for self-torment; a leader returns to the task with renewed effort, because exertion, not fate alone, brings results.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LVI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: exertion and destiny operate together but exertion is superior, since destiny is inferred from results of effort; do not grieve if what you began ends badly, exert yourself in it with redoubled attention.

The constituted text sets the verse after a call to constant exertion (utthāna); its second line instead commends discipline (vinaya) as the king's highest policy, so "try again" rests on the vulgate reading.

practical_reading: For anyone leading a project: when it fails, skip the self-punishment, review, and re-engage with more care; that is what responsibility looks like.
misreadings: Not "never feel disappointed"; it targets the self-torment that stops the next attempt.
Not "repeat the same thing blindly"; Ganguli stresses redoubled attention.
cautions: Addressed to a king about statecraft; frame for leaders, parents, managers rather than as universal pressure to keep trying.
speaks_to: a failed launch, campaign, exam or project
managers and team leads after a setback
not_for: someone whose "undertaking" was a relationship that ended for good reason
burnout
research_note: Our prasang is null for this verse; the setting text is accurate.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.81.16 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXX (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Our reading vṛddhyā na tapyeta ("is not pained by your rise") gives the natural sense and matches Ganguli's paraphrase of the passage (a friend fears your calamity and rejoices at your prosperity). BORI reads samṛddhyā na tuṣyeta, which is awkward. Translation fine.
context: Yudhishthira asks what a king's counsellor should be like and whom to trust. Bhishma lists kinds of friends, warns that anyone can turn and that total trust ruins while total distrust is like death, gives the marks of an enemy and of the best friend, then turns to kinsmen: fear them like death, since a kinsman cannot bear a kinsman's rise, yet the kinless are easily overrun; honour them in word and act while privately staying wary. This verse comes right after the marks of an enemy (one who thinks your loss will bring him gain).

key_terms.sense: is not stung (with envy) by your growth

core_teaching: The surest mark of a true friend is that your success does not sting them and your losses grieve them.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXX)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one whose fall would follow yours should be trusted like a father; a friend is like your own self who fears when calamity strikes you and rejoices at your prosperity; those who wish you harm are foes.
In the constituted text the best-friend verse sits among warnings that friends change, that one should trust and suspect selectively, and that an enemy is one who expects to gain by your loss.

practical_reading: Use it as a mirror more than a test: can I be glad, not threatened, when a friend does well, and truly sorry when they struggle?
misreadings: Not a tool for suspicion ("prove you're not jealous").
Not "friends must never feel envy"; the mark is how they act on it.
cautions: Context is a king's guide to trust and suspicion, not a warm essay on friendship.
speaks_to: someone hurt that a friend wasn't happy for them
not_for: someone already paranoid about friends
a reader grieving a lost friendship

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.81.35 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXX (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate. Literally: a kinsman never tolerates the humiliation of a kinsman by outsiders.
context: Yudhishthira asks what a king's counsellor should be like and whom to trust. Bhishma lists kinds of friends, warns that anyone can turn and that total trust ruins while total distrust is like death, gives the marks of an enemy and of the best friend, then turns to kinsmen: fear them like death, since a kinsman cannot bear a kinsman's rise, yet the kinless are easily overrun; honour them in word and act while privately staying wary. The very next verse adds that one also knows oneself wronged by one's own kin; there are virtues and faults in them.
core_teaching: For all their friction, kin are the refuge when outsiders wrong you, because they feel the insult as their own.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXX)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: fear kinsmen as death, for they cannot bear your prosperity; yet the kinless are despised and overrun; kinsmen are the refuge of one afflicted by others; honour them while privately wary.
Constituted text: the verse is balanced by the next, which admits one is also wronged by kin and that both good and bad are seen among them; hence honour them in word and deed.

practical_reading: A reminder that family conflicts can coexist with deep loyalty; when the world turns on you, the people who share your name often show up.
misreadings: Not "family is always safe" (our own note is right).
Not a reason to tolerate mistreatment at home.
cautions: Must not be shown to someone wronged by their own family.
Bhishma's surrounding advice includes outward trust with inner mistrust of kin; not a model of healthy family life.
speaks_to: someone humiliated at work or in public whose family rallied
reconciling with relatives after a feud
not_for: domestic abuse or family estrangement
LGBTQ readers rejected by family
someone without family

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.82.21 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXXI (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Narada to Krishna, as retold by Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Mostly accurate. "Giving food and help" adds "help": the text says giving food according to one's capacity. BORI reads dama (self-restraint) where we have mārdava (gentleness); Ganguli has mildness.
context: Bhishma tells how Krishna confided in Narada about his own clan: he gives them half of what he has and bears their cruel words, which grind his heart like fire-sticks, and he is caught between rival factions like the mother of two gamblers. Narada says the trouble is internal and partly of Krishna's own making, and that force would bring slaughter, so he should use a soft weapon to correct his kinsmen's tongues and carry the burden of leadership like a strong ox on a rough road. Krishna asks what this weapon is; this verse is Narada's answer.

key_terms.sense: feeding others as far as one can
a weapon not made of iron

core_teaching: To hold a quarrelsome family together, the effective weapon is not force but steady generosity, forbearance, sincerity, gentleness and due respect to each person.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: giving food as one can, forgiveness, sincerity, mildness and honour where due are a weapon not of steel; Narada adds that the calamity is internal, born of Krishna's own acts, and only the strong carry such loads.
Constituted text lists titikṣā and dama (restraint) beside sincerity; the episode frames this as advice to the head of a clan on preventing internal destruction, not to a victim.

practical_reading: For whoever holds a family or team together: feed people, absorb some provocation, be straight and gentle, and give each their due; these win more than confrontation.
misreadings: Patience with family is not tolerating abuse (our misuse note is right).
Not passivity: Narada calls it a weapon to be sharpened and used.
cautions: Counsel to the person with power and responsibility in the family, not to one being harmed by it (our note is right).
speaks_to: eldest siblings, parents and heads of households managing feuds
someone tired of being the peacemaker
not_for: someone being abused or controlled by family
a child or dependent told to keep the peace

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.82.22 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXXI (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Narada to Krishna, as retold by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate. Sanskrit typos: लधूनि should be लघूनि (laghūni, "petty, light"), and शमयस्य should be शमयस्व (śamayasva, "calm!"). BORI: kaṭūni ca laghūni ca.
context: Bhishma tells how Krishna confided in Narada about his own clan: he gives them half of what he has and bears their cruel words, which grind his heart like fire-sticks, and he is caught between rival factions like the mother of two gamblers. Narada says the trouble is internal and partly of Krishna's own making, and that force would bring slaughter, so he should use a soft weapon to correct his kinsmen's tongues and carry the burden of leadership like a strong ox on a rough road. This verse continues the description of the soft weapon.

key_terms.sense: about to speak, wanting to say

core_teaching: When relatives are on the verge of saying bitter or petty things, use your own words to settle their hearts, speech and minds before the quarrel starts.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: with soft words alone turn away the anger of kinsmen about to utter cruel speeches, and mollify their hearts, minds and slanderous tongues; take up the weight of leading the clan.
Constituted text reads kaṭūni ca laghūni ca and śamayasva, confirming the meaning; it continues Narada's soft-weapon list for a leader keeping a clan from splitting.

practical_reading: De-escalate early: when you sense a family gathering heading for a fight, a warm, timely word can defuse it before anyone says what they will regret.
misreadings: Not "always swallow your truth"; it is about timing and tone.
Not the responsibility of a child or a victim to manage adults' anger.
cautions: Same as the previous verse: advice to the one with standing in the family.
not_for: someone facing verbal abuse at home
people-pleasers who already over-manage others' moods

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.85.5-6 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXXIV (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Brihaspati to Indra (Shakra), retold by Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate. Sanskrit typo: भुकुटीमुखः should be भ्रुकुटीमुखः (bhrukuṭī, frown). BORI has satatam for sarvadā and pūrvam abhiprekṣya for sarvam abhiprekṣya; same sense.
context: Bhishma recounts how Indra asked Brihaspati for the one thing that makes a person loved by all and famous. Brihaspati answers: conciliatory, pleasant speech (sāntva). He adds that a gift without kind words pleases no one, that even people deprived of their goods can be reconciled by sweet speech, and that a king who must punish should still speak gently. Bhishma tells Yudhishthira to practise it.

key_terms.sense: speaks first, takes the initiative to greet
one who speaks with a smile

core_teaching: Warm, welcoming speech is the single practice that wins general goodwill: the silent frowner is disliked, while one who greets first with a smile is loved.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: agreeableness of speech is the one thing that wins regard from all; the silent, frowning man is hated, while one who addresses others first with smiles gratifies everyone.
Constituted text matches; the short chapter also says even those whose goods are taken can be reconciled by gentle words, showing sāntva as a political skill as well as a courtesy.

practical_reading: Be the one who greets first: a smile and an opening word at work, home or a new place changes how people receive you.
misreadings: Not flattery or manipulation, even though the passage notes sweet speech can soften people who have been wronged.
Not a judgment on quiet or shy people.
cautions: Can sting for socially anxious or depressed readers who find smiling hard; frame as a small practice, not a verdict.
speaks_to: starting at a new job, school or neighbourhood
someone noticing they come across as cold
not_for: social anxiety or depression framed as a fault
someone told to smile at an abuser

attribution_note: Brihaspati to Indra, retold by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate. Ganguli: "like rice without curry".

Bhishma tells Yudhishthira to practise it. This verse follows the smile-and-speak-first verse.
core_teaching: How you give matters as much as what you give: a gift without warmth pleases no one, like a meal with no seasoning.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: even gifts made without agreeable speech do not delight, like rice without curry; sweetness of speech never fails and never pains any heart.
Same wording in the constituted text; vyañjana is the condiment or relish served with rice.

practical_reading: When you help or give, add the words: a note, a kind sentence, attention. Help delivered coldly can feel like a transaction or a humiliation.
misreadings: Not "words matter more than real help"; the gift is still the food.
speaks_to: caregivers and parents who give a lot but feel unappreciated
not_for: someone in need being told to be grateful for cold help

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.104.33 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section CIII (wisdomlib). Close parallel at BORI 12.138.64 (Bharadvaja to the Sauvira king).
attribution_note: Brihaspati to Indra, retold by Bhishma to Yudhishthira; confirmed in BORI and Ganguli.
translation_note: Literal: do not be (only) harsh, do not be (only) soft; be harsh, be soft. Ganguli: be both fierce and mild. Our "when needed" gloss is supported by the parallel 12.138.64, which says harsh at the time for harshness, soft at the time for softness.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a king should deal with a mild enemy, a fierce one, and one with many allies. Bhishma retells Brihaspati's advice to Indra: hide hostility behind sweet words, wait for the right moment, use spies and division, attack enemies one at a time. This verse sits in that hard-edged statecraft.
core_teaching: People disregard a leader who is only soft and recoil from one who is only harsh; authority needs both, each at its proper time.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a mild king is disregarded, a fierce one inspires dread, so be neither only fierce nor only mild but both; it sits amid advice on concealment, timing and dividing enemies.
The same maxim reappears in Bharadvaja's counsel (12.138.64), which spells out the timing: harsh when it is time for harshness, gentle when it is time for gentleness.

practical_reading: For parents, managers and teachers: kindness without boundaries gets ignored, boundaries without kindness breed fear. Read the moment.
misreadings: Firmness means clarity and consequences, not cruelty (our misuse note is right).
Not license to be unpredictable or manipulative.
cautions: From advice on handling enemies by deceit and force; take only the balance principle.
speaks_to: someone who is a pushover or too harsh
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship being told to be gentler
readers seeking justification for harshness

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.105.16 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section CIV (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: The sage Kalakavrikshiya to Prince Kshemadarshi of Kosala, retold by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate. BORI: abhūtvā ca bhavaty api and śokaṃ kuryāt kathaṃ naraḥ, same sense. Ganguli: things that were are no more, grief has no power to restore them.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, army and treasury should find happiness. Bhishma tells of Prince Kshemadarshi of Kosala, who, after failing to win back his kingdom, asks the sage Kalakavrikshiya what he can do short of suicide, theft or begging refuge. The sage says all possessions are unstable, grief cannot restore them, wise people want only what is attainable and bear others' prosperity, and he could live contentedly alone in the forest. In the next section the sage offers a strategy for recovering the kingdom if the prince still has the strength, and later reconciles him with King Janaka. This verse comes early in the sage's first reply, after he tells the prince that what earlier generations acquired has all perished.

key_terms.sense: having been, it ceases to be
having not been, it will come to be

core_teaching: Things arise and pass by their nature; grief has no power to reverse that, so endless grieving over what is gone is futile.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: everything acquired by forebears has perished; things that were are no more and grief cannot restore them; where are your father and grandfather? Everyone now twenty or thirty will be dead within a century.
Constituted text matches. The prince's question openly lists suicide among the options he wants to avoid, which frames the whole consolation.

practical_reading: After losing a job, status or money: grieve, but notice that rumination cannot change the fact; redirect energy to what can still be done.
misreadings: Feeling grief is human; the point is not to feed it endlessly (our misuse note is right).
Counsel about lost wealth and position, not a death (our note is right).
cautions: The prince has mentioned suicide as an option he is trying to avoid; never quote the setting for a distressed reader.
The sage's reasoning also invokes dead parents and everyone's death; it can feel cold.
speaks_to: job loss, business failure, lost status
someone stuck replaying a financial loss
not_for: fresh bereavement
suicidal thoughts

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: never grieve for past or future; desiring only the obtainable, enjoy present possessions and do not mourn what is absent; be glad of what you win with ease, and keep a pure disposition.

practical_reading: A grounding practice for anxious or deprived seasons: list what is within reach and enjoyable today, and catch yourself pre-grieving imagined futures.
misreadings: Not "stop hoping or planning"; it is about longing for the impossible and anticipatory grief.
cautions: Same frame as the previous verse (a ruined prince); may sound dismissive to someone facing real scarcity.
speaks_to: someone fixated on a lost or unattainable goal
not_for: people in poverty told to want less
fresh grief

translation_note: Lines 1-2 accurate. Line 3 in our Sanskrit looks corrupt; the translation follows its evident sense, which Ganguli confirms. The meaning of kuśalāḥ is disputed (see commentaries).
context: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, army and treasury should find happiness. Bhishma tells of Prince Kshemadarshi of Kosala, who, after failing to win back his kingdom, asks the sage Kalakavrikshiya what he can do short of suicide, theft or begging refuge. The sage says all possessions are unstable, grief cannot restore them, wise people want only what is attainable and bear others' prosperity, and he could live contentedly alone in the forest. In the next section the sage offers a strategy for recovering the kingdom if the prince still has the strength, and later reconciles him with King Janaka. Here the sage says a foolish man stripped of fortune blames the Ordainer and resents others' undeserved prosperity; the prince is free of that vice, so he should bear others' good fortune.

key_terms.sense: bear, tolerate, the prosperity of others
skilful; or (per Nilakantha) free from envy
fortune that lies elsewhere, with someone else

core_teaching: Make peace with other people's good fortune even when you lack it; the wise can take joy in fortune that is not theirs, while resentment drives fortune away.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli: endure others' prosperity though you have none; the dexterous enjoy prosperity vested in others; prosperity leaves one who hates others.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha, as reported in Ganguli's note 5
commentaries.gist: Nilakantha glosses kuśala as "free from envy" and "elsewhere" as "in an enemy": the non-envious can enjoy fortune even when it sits with a rival. Ganguli says he does not follow this.
Only the first two lines are in the constituted text (reading janāḥ for narāḥ); the line about fortune draining from the resentful is absent there.

practical_reading: A practice against envy: when someone else succeeds, try sharing in it (mudita) rather than measuring yourself; resentment only adds a second loss.
misreadings: Not "accept injustice"; it addresses envy, not unfairness.
Not a promise that being gracious brings money back.
cautions: Line 3 is textually weak; avoid building a reading on it.
speaks_to: envy of peers' success (promotions, weddings, babies)
someone recovering from a setback while others thrive
not_for: someone whose "rival" harmed them
infertility or loss where others' joy is acutely painful
research_note: Third Sanskrit line not in BORI and looks corrupt in our data.
