context: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, army and treasury should find happiness. Bhishma tells of Prince Kshemadarshi of Kosala, who, after failing to win back his kingdom, asks the sage Kalakavrikshiya what he can do short of suicide, theft or begging refuge. The sage says all possessions are unstable, grief cannot restore them, wise people want only what is attainable and bear others' prosperity, and he could live contentedly alone in the forest. In the next section the sage offers a strategy for recovering the kingdom if the prince still has the strength, and later reconciles him with King Janaka. This image comes in the sage's closing advice to live alone and content in the forest; he says a person in the prince's plight can live happily so. The next section offers a political route back instead.

key_terms.sense: becomes clear and calm by itself

core_teaching: A deep lake stirred up clears by itself; likewise one whose understanding is formed regains clarity from within, without forcing.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a large turbid lake resumes tranquillity of itself; a wise man disturbed by such matters becomes tranquil of himself. The sage pairs this with life alone in the forest, compassionate and content.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.105.52 and star passage 246 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Only the lake half-line is in the constituted text; the explicit comparison to the wise person is a manuscript addition, as our backticks show.

practical_reading: When upset, stop stirring: give the mind stillness and let understanding do its work, the way silt settles when the water is left alone.
misreadings: Not "just wait, time heals": it is wisdom that settles the mind (our note is right; the line is not).
Not "suppress feelings".
cautions: In context tied to withdrawing alone to the forest; do not suggest isolation to a struggling reader.
speaks_to: anger or agitation after a blow-up
not_for: clinical depression where waiting it out is unsafe advice
someone who needs to act urgently
research_note: Fix the line so it does not say "given time".

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.109.3 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section CVIII (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate ("bahumatā mama" is "is most esteemed by me"). BORI reads atra yukto ("one devoted to this") for atra vartan.
context: Yudhishthira asks which of the many branches of duty matters most. Bhishma names honouring mother, father and teacher. He goes straight on to say their commands should be followed whether or not they accord with dharma, likens the three to the three sacred fires, ranks the mother above ten fathers and the teacher above both, and says parents should never be slain or punished even if they offend.
core_teaching: Of the many duties, Bhishma rates honouring one's mother, father and teachers as foremost; living by it brings both good standing and spiritual reward.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: worship of mother, father and preceptor is most important; their commands should be done whether consistent with righteousness or not; they are the three fires; the mother outweighs ten fathers, yet the teacher outranks both.
Constituted text keeps the obedience verses immediately after this one, so the library's choice to stop at 109.3 is a real editorial cut.

practical_reading: A call to gratitude and respect toward those who raised and taught us: visiting, caring for aging parents, thanking teachers.
misreadings: Not obedience into harm (our misuse note is right; the very next verses ask for it, which is why they are cut).
Not a ranking of people's worth.
cautions: Surrounding verses demand obedience even against dharma and say parents should go unpunished whatever they do; never pair with readers from abusive or controlling homes.
Can feel like guilt for adult children setting boundaries.
not_for: survivors of parental abuse
estranged children
someone pressured by family to give up a choice

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.114.9 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section CXIII (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: The river Ganga to the Ocean, retold by Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate. BORI: namati netaraḥ ("no other bends") and sthānam āsādya tiṣṭhati ("it regains its place and stands"), same sense.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a king without allies should behave toward a far stronger enemy. Bhishma tells how the Ocean asked the rivers why they carry away great trees but never the reeds on their banks. Ganga answers that rigid trees resist and are uprooted, while the reed bends to the flood, knows time and place, and rises after. Bhishma concludes that one who will not yield to an overwhelming foe is destroyed, and the wise adopt the reed's conduct.
core_teaching: Flexibility under overwhelming force is survival, not defeat: bend while the flood passes, then stand again where you were.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the cane bows to the current and resumes its posture after; it knows time and opportunity. Bhishma: whoever will not yield to a mightier foe soon perishes. Ganguli's note: true policy is waiting till the foe weakens.

The weak king attacked by a powerful one should live like a reed in a current, an opinion credited to Bharadvaja; Kautilya qualifies it: bowing to everyone breeds despair, so seek a strong protector or a fortress.
Same parable in the constituted text; it is framed as statecraft for a weak ruler facing a stronger enemy.

practical_reading: In a crisis you cannot win head-on (a layoff wave, an illness, a market crash), adapt, conserve and wait, without abandoning who you are.
misreadings: Bending under pressure is not giving up your values (our misuse note is right).
Not a rule to submit to mistreatment (our note is right); it is strategy for surviving overwhelming force.
cautions: Do not give to someone in an abusive relationship as advice to "bend".
not_for: abuse, harassment or coercion
someone being pressured to compromise their integrity

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.115.7cdef (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section CXIV (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Translation follows the right sense. Sanskrit typo: प्रकृत्या ("by nature") should be प्राकृतो (prākṛtaḥ, "a vulgar, common person"), as in BORI and Ganguli ("a vulgar fellow"). BORI reads vāśamāno for vāśyamāno.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a modest, learned man should respond when a conceited fool abuses him in an assembly. Bhishma: one who bears abuse without anger takes the abuser's merit; abusive talk is like a bird's harsh cry; such a man boasts of his insults; then this verse. The slanderer only exposes his own nature; avoid him, and do not trade words, since a quarrel between the high and the low is disapproved by the calm.
core_teaching: The praise or blame of a thoughtless person has no real power over you; it is noise, like a crow cawing in the forest.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: what can a vulgar fellow do by praise or blame? He is a crow cawing uselessly in the woods; if mere words could prove accusations they would matter; the slanderer only displays his own nature; avoid him.
The constituted text reads prākṛto ("a common person"), confirming that the verse is about an unthinking critic, not about everyone's opinion.

practical_reading: For online abuse or public insults: you do not owe a response to noise. Save your energy for criticism that comes from thought and goodwill.
misreadings: Fair criticism is worth hearing (our misuse note is right).
Not contempt for ordinary people; prākṛta here means the thoughtless abuser.
cautions: The surrounding passage uses harsh labels for the abuser (bastardy, dog); keep the reading calm.
If the "abuse" is harassment or threats, ignoring it may not be safe; real help comes first.
speaks_to: people-pleasers hooked on approval (praise too is noise)
not_for: harassment or threats needing action
someone dismissing legitimate feedback

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.136.45 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section CXXXVIII (wisdomlib). Note our chapter is two higher than BORI here.
attribution_note: The mouse Palita, thinking to himself, in the story Bhishma tells Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Only the first half is translated. The second half says: my life now rests on my enemy, the cat. Without it the maxim loses its point (an emergency alliance with a natural enemy). BORI reads śreyān ("better") and apaṇḍitam.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a king surrounded by enemies keeps his wits. Bhishma tells of the mouse Palita, who finds a cat caught in a hunter's net, a mongoose below and an owl above. Reasoning that a cornered enemy may make peace, he says this verse to himself, then offers to gnaw the cat free in exchange for protection. Both keep the deal, but afterwards the mouse refuses the cat's friendship, arguing that alliances rest on interest.

key_terms.sense: my life rests on my enemy

core_teaching: In a crisis, an intelligent adversary who understands shared interest is a better partner than a well-meaning fool; the mouse bets his life on that.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXXXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one afflicted by a stronger foe should make peace even with an enemy; better a learned enemy than a fool for a friend; my life is in the cat's hands, so let me address him about his own liberation.
In the constituted text the mouse calls the cat a fool just before and hopes alliance may make him a wise enemy; the maxim is tactical self-talk in apaddharma, not a general rule.

practical_reading: In negotiations or emergencies, judge partners by competence and aligned interest, not by sentiment; and choose wise counsel even when it comes from someone you dislike.
misreadings: Not "ditch kind but simple friends".
Not a call to trust enemies; the mouse stays wary throughout.
cautions: The story's closing moral is cynical: friendships are interest-based. Use for strategy, not for questions about real friendship.
not_for: someone hurt by a friend's foolish mistake
loneliness
research_note: Translation omits the second half-verse.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.138.65 (BORI); Ganguli, Santi Parva section CXL (wisdomlib).
attribution_note: The brahmin Kaninka of the Bharadvaja line to the Sauvira king, retold by Bhishma. The king is Shatrunjaya in Ganguli but Shatruntapa in BORI.
translation_note: "Hanti" is literally "strikes down, destroys": with softness one destroys the soft and the harsh. "Overcomes" is an acceptable softening, but the passage is about prevailing over enemies. BORI: tīkṣṇataraṃ mṛdu.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a king should act in a decaying age beset by robbers. Bhishma says he will describe policy for hard times, "setting compassion aside", via Kaninka's counsel to the Sauvira king: keep the rod ready, be humble in speech but razor-sharp at heart, make peace without trusting, cut enemies at the root. Just before this verse: people despise the soft and fear the harsh, so be harsh at the time for harshness and soft at the time for softness. Kaninka ends by saying this conduct is only for times of distress.
core_teaching: Gentleness, used well, prevails over both gentle and fierce opponents; nothing is beyond it, which makes it sharper than harshness.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXL)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: be stern when sternness is needed, mild when mildness is; by mildness the mild are cut and the fierce destroyed; nothing mildness cannot effect, so it is sharper than fierceness. All this is for seasons of distress.
The constituted text frames the counsel as policy for calamity with compassion set aside, opens with the ever-raised rod, and places this verse after the be-harsh-or-soft-in-season maxim.

practical_reading: In conflict, calm and courteous persistence often achieves more than force: it disarms the hostile and does not provoke resistance.
misreadings: Not a teaching on meekness (our note is right): gentleness here is a means of prevailing.
Not "soft is always enough"; the preceding verse says be harsh when it is time.
cautions: Comes from a ruthless, explicitly compassion-suspending speech; do not present Kaninka as a gentle sage.
speaks_to: dealing with difficult colleagues or customers
not_for: someone in an abusive situation being told to be gentler
readers seeking manipulation tactics
research_note: King's name differs between editions (Shatrunjaya vs Shatruntapa).

verified_ref: Not in the BORI constituted text: BORI star passage 366 (lines 1-2), inserted after 12.142.7. Ganguli, Santi Parva section CXLIV (wisdomlib) includes it.
attribution_note: The male pigeon lamenting to himself. Nested: Bhishma to Yudhishthira, retelling what Parashurama (Bhargava) told King Muchukunda.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Yudhishthira asks about the merit of protecting one who seeks refuge. Bhishma tells a story that Parashurama (Bhargava) once told King Muchukunda: in a storm a fowler, who has caged a female pigeon, shelters under a tree where her mate lives. The male pigeon laments his missing wife; she, in the cage, urges him to honour the fowler as a guest. He welcomes the fowler, lights a fire for him and, having no food, throws himself into it as a meal. The shaken fowler frees the female, who then also enters the fire; the fowler renounces his trade and later dies in a forest fire, and all three reach heaven. This verse is in the male pigeon's lament that night, before he knows his wife is caged below.
core_teaching: Home is where the beloved is; without them even a palace is a wilderness.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXLIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a house is not a home, the wife is the home; even the foot of a tree is home with one's spouse, and without her a palace is a desolate wilderness. The praise includes her never eating or sitting before him.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.142.4-10 and star passages 364-368 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted lament keeps the core (empty home, no medicine or ally like a wife); the tree-and-palace couplet and much of the praise are manuscript additions.

practical_reading: Used for couples and families who have moved, downsized or live simply: belonging is in the relationship, not the building.
misreadings: Not the wife's duty to be the husband's "home" at her own expense.
cautions: The surrounding praise idealises a wife who never eats before her husband, and the story ends with the widowed pigeon throwing herself into the fire because she cannot live without him. Never use this story for widowhood or partner loss.
The pigeon fears his wife is lost; for someone whose partner has died or left, it can deepen pain.
speaks_to: couples who have moved, migrated or downsized
not_for: widowhood or recent partner loss
divorce

going abroad, travel far from home
one who gives confidence, the trusted one

core_teaching: A spouse is a partner across every sphere of life and the one you can rely on when far from home.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXLIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the spouse is one's associate in virtue, profit and pleasure, the trusted companion abroad, the best medicine in sickness; there is no friend or refuge like a wife.
This couplet is a manuscript addition, but the constituted text says the same in its own words: a wife is the companion on life's road, the best medicine, the best ally in dharma.

practical_reading: For marriage reflection: a partner is a companion in values, work and joy alike; trust is built for the times you are far from home.
misreadings: Not a statement that a woman's worth is in serving her husband.
cautions: Same story cautions as the previous verse (self-immolation of both pigeons; widow cannot live without husband).
speaks_to: partners supporting each other through moves or work abroad
not_for: widowhood or partner loss
readers in unhappy or controlling marriages
singles who feel judged
research_note: Not in the critical text.

verified_ref: Not in the BORI constituted text: BORI star passage 374, after 12.142.24. Ganguli, Santi Parva section CXLVI (wisdomlib) includes it. Our chapter number 145 matches neither.
attribution_note: The male pigeon to the fowler (nested in Bhishma's retelling of Parashurama's story to Muchukunda).
translation_note: Accurate: hospitality is due even to an enemy who comes to your home. Our line ("Be kind even to one who wronged you") broadens it beyond the guest who seeks shelter, which our own note warns against.
context: Yudhishthira asks about the merit of protecting one who seeks refuge. Bhishma tells a story that Parashurama (Bhargava) once told King Muchukunda: in a storm a fowler, who has caged a female pigeon, shelters under a tree where her mate lives. The male pigeon laments his missing wife; she, in the cage, urges him to honour the fowler as a guest. He welcomes the fowler, lights a fire for him and, having no food, throws himself into it as a meal. The shaken fowler frees the female, who then also enters the fire; the fowler renounces his trade and later dies in a forest fire, and all three reach heaven. Here the pigeon, urged by his caged wife, greets the cold fowler as a guest who has sought refuge, then lights a fire and offers himself as food.

key_terms.sense: one who has come to your home
one who seeks refuge (the frame of the passage)

core_teaching: Duty to a guest who seeks shelter does not depend on who he is: as a tree shades even the woodcutter, hospitality is owed even to an enemy at your door.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXLVI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: you are welcome, this is your home; hospitality should be shown even to a foe; the tree does not withdraw its shade from one who comes to cut it; a householder of the five sacrifices is especially bound.
The constituted text grounds the welcome in duty to one who has sought refuge and the householder's five daily offerings; the tree-and-shade couplet itself is a manuscript addition.

practical_reading: Basic dignity and care are owed even to people we dislike when they come to us in need: the stranger, the rival, the difficult relative at the door.
misreadings: Kindness is not letting someone keep harming you (our misuse note is right).
Not a general rule to be kind to whoever harms you (our note is right; the line drifts toward it).
cautions: In the story this hospitality ends in the pigeon's self-sacrifice in the fire, followed by his widow's; never let the reading glorify self-destruction.
Do not offer to someone being harmed by the "guest".
speaks_to: humanitarian work with people seen as enemies
professionals (doctors, lawyers) serving people they dislike
not_for: abuse survivors
someone being told to keep sheltering a person who hurts them
suicidal readers (story context)
research_note: Not in the critical text; consider adjusting the line to keep the guest/refuge frame.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.167.19 (BORI constituted text; also repeated in star passage 449). Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXIII (wisdomlib). Our chapter is five higher than BORI.
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira, closing a story he heard from Narada.
translation_note: The translation drops the final clause "kṛtaghne nāsti niṣkṛtiḥ" (for the ungrateful there is no expiation), which is the point Bhishma stresses (expiations exist for grave sins, none for ingratitude). The line reorders the logic, making trust the cause of the other losses.
context: Bhishma ends the tale of Gautama, a destitute brahmin who was fed and sheltered by the crane Rajadharman and enriched by the crane's friend, the Rakshasa king Virupaksha, then killed his sleeping host for food on the way home. Virupaksha has Gautama killed; the crane is revived by the divine cow Surabhi and asks Indra to revive Gautama too; Gautama goes home and is later cursed to hell. Bhishma, who heard it from Narada, draws the lesson about ingratitude and friendship. After this verse he adds that one must never betray a friend, should always be grateful, and that everything, including help in danger, comes through friends.

key_terms.sense: ungrateful, one who destroys what was done for him

core_teaching: Ingratitude destroys a person's name, standing and peace, because no one can trust him; the text treats it as a wrong with no ritual expiation.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CLXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: whence can an ungrateful person have fame, place or happiness? He is not to be trusted and can never escape; no one should injure a friend; be grateful, since everything comes through friends.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.167.16-21 and star passage 449 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: In the constituted text; a longer manuscript version adds that expiations exist for killing a brahmin or drinking liquor but none for ingratitude.

practical_reading: Remember who helped you and honour it; trust, once broken by using people and discarding them, is hard to rebuild.
misreadings: Not a tool to demand gratitude from people we have helped.
Not "you owe your abuser"; gratitude is for real kindness.
cautions: "Ungrateful" is often used to silence children or partners leaving controlling situations; never pair with them.
The story has a killing, caste-laden language and a curse to hell; keep the reading on the principle.
speaks_to: reflecting on how we treat benefactors and mentors
repairing a relationship after taking someone for granted
not_for: abuse survivors told they are ungrateful
depressed readers who cannot feel gratitude and blame themselves
research_note: Translation omits the "no expiation" clause.

verified_ref: Not in the BORI constituted text: BORI star passage 449 (lines 40-41), appended after 12.167.21 in some manuscripts. Not clearly rendered in Ganguli section CLXXIII (wisdomlib), which has a looser equivalent.
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira (the star passage is headed "Bhishma said").
translation_note: Accurate for our Sanskrit. The line's "Money comes and goes" is not in the verse, which says money is easily obtained through friends.
context: Bhishma ends the tale of Gautama, a destitute brahmin who was fed and sheltered by the crane Rajadharman and enriched by the crane's friend, the Rakshasa king Virupaksha, then killed his sleeping host for food on the way home. Virupaksha has Gautama killed; the crane is revived by the divine cow Surabhi and asks Indra to revive Gautama too; Gautama goes home and is later cursed to hell. Bhishma, who heard it from Narada, draws the lesson about ingratitude and friendship. This couplet belongs to a longer manuscript version of Bhishma's closing lesson on friendship; the constituted text and Ganguli say more briefly that strength and every good come through friends.

key_terms.sense: with a friend one is able to strive

core_teaching: A friend is worth more than money: wealth comes easily through friends, and a friend makes effort possible.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CLXXIII, n. 3)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: everything may be obtained from or through a friend, honours, enjoyments, escape from danger; the wise honour friends. His note explains the ablative as both "from" and "through" friends.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.167.21 and star passage 449 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text: be grateful and friend-seeking; truth and strength arise from a friend. This exact couplet appears only in the manuscript expansion, which also says a friend is called true wealth.

practical_reading: Invest in friendships as you would in savings: relationships open doors and give courage that money alone cannot.
misreadings: Not "make friends for what they can get you"; it praises friendship over wealth.
cautions: Comes at the end of a story of betrayal and murder; keep the reading on friendship.
speaks_to: someone choosing between a career move and staying near friends
not_for: someone just betrayed by a friend
isolated readers who may feel shamed for having few friends
research_note: Weakly attested verse (manuscript addition only).

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.173.21 in the vulgate numbering used by Sanskrit Wikisource (our numbering matches it); BORI critical edition 12.168.19; Ganguli Santi section CLXXIV.
attribution_note: The brahmin to King Senajit, inside Bhishma's narration to Yudhishthira. Ganguli calls him a brahmin friend of the king; BORI only says 'a certain brahmin'.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; he first tells the king that he too will soon be mourned, that people meet and part like two logs drifting on the ocean, and that joy and sorrow follow each other. This verse closes that point; the vulgate line just before says joy and sorrow turn like a wheel. The talk then moves to the body as the seat of pleasure and pain and to letting go of craving.

key_terms.sense: you have fallen from happiness into sorrow

core_teaching: Happiness and sorrow take turns in every life, so the present sorrow is not permanent; neither state is held for ever.

commentaries.gist: The brahmin's ground is that nothing, not even his own self, is truly 'his', and that unions are like driftwood that meets and parts; Ganguli's note adds that joy and grief end with the body.

Both set this verse right after the claim that sorrow follows happiness and happiness follows sorrow; the vulgate adds the wheel image, which BORI keeps only as a manuscript addition (star passage 460).
Same wording in the constituted text; the episode is the opening of the Mokshadharma, answering how to dispel grief at loss.

practical_reading: When a hard season feels endless, remember that states change; this is a reason to hold on, not a promise about timing.
misreadings: Not a promise that a specific loss will be undone or 'made up for'.
Not an instruction to stop feeling grief now.
cautions: Spoken to a father whose son has just died; the surrounding speech calls him deluded and says one should not feel affection for children because separation is certain. Use this verse alone, not its frame, for grieving parents.
'You will be happy again' can feel dismissive in the first days of a bereavement.
speaks_to: a long low patch after a job loss, breakup or failure
someone who feels stuck in a bad season
people who need perspective that moods and fortunes change
not_for: a parent in the first weeks after a child's death
chronic illness or depression where 'it will pass' sounds like minimising

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.173.40 (Sanskrit Wikisource, vulgate numbering); BORI 12.168.29. A near-identical line also stands at BORI 12.27.30 in Vyasa's consolation of Yudhishthira.
attribution_note: The brahmin to Senajit, narrated by Bhishma.
translation_note: A fair literal rendering. Note that the first half is ambiguous: Ganguli splits it as 'happiness ends in misery; idleness is misery', and Nilakantha records a variant reading.
context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; after describing how only the wise who have gone beyond pairs of opposites stay untroubled, he turns to effort: idleness is pleasant and ends in pain, capable effort is painful and ends in joy. The next verses tell the king to meet whatever comes with an undefeated heart.

key_terms.sense: capability, diligent skill / the capable person
prosperity/power and good fortune (Nilakantha: yogic powers and knowledge)

core_teaching: Ease that avoids effort ends in sorrow, while capable effort, though hard, leads to happiness; good fortune stays with the diligent.

commentaries.gist: Reads it spiritually: idleness means not taking up the means to knowledge; prosperity means yogic powers and fortune means knowledge. Records a variant first line.
Parses the first half as two statements, that happiness ends in misery and that idleness is misery, with cleverness in action the cause of happiness; prosperity lives with the capable.
The same maxim appears twice in the Shanti Parva consolations, once in Vyasa's speech to Yudhishthira and once here, which shows it was a stock saying.

practical_reading: Notice which comforts are really avoidance; do the slightly hard thing today that your future self will thank you for.
misreadings: Not a glorification of overwork or hustle.
Not a judgement on rest, illness or depression; Nilakantha's reading is about neglecting the spiritual path.
cautions: Comes in a consolation to a bereaved father; do not use it to tell a grieving person to 'get busy'.
Can shame people with low energy from illness or depression.
speaks_to: someone choosing between comfort and a demanding goal
students and early-career people building habits
not_for: burnout or exhaustion
depression, chronic fatigue or illness
fresh grief

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.173.41 (Sanskrit Wikisource); BORI 12.168.30, which reads 'dveṣyaṃ vā' (hateful) for 'apriyam' (unpleasant), same sense. Also at BORI 12.26.26 in Vyasa's speech.
attribution_note: The brahmin to Senajit, narrated by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Upāsīta' covers both enjoying and enduring what comes, as Ganguli brings out.
context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; right after saying that effort, not idleness, brings fortune, he gives this rule for meeting events: take each as it comes without being conquered by it. The next verse says thousands of occasions for grief and fear daily overwhelm the undiscerning, but not the wise.

key_terms.sense: whatever arrives, each thing in turn

core_teaching: Meet each pleasant or painful thing as it actually arrives, without letting joy or sorrow take control of the heart.

commentaries.gist: Pleasant and unpleasant are what produce joy and pain; 'undefeated' means not brought under the sway of a heart made of elation and grief.
Renders it as enjoying or enduring what comes with an unconquered heart, placed between the praise of capable effort and the warning about daily causes of grief.
The same couplet occurs in Vyasa's consolation of Yudhishthira as well as here, so it is a recurring teaching of the Shanti Parva consolations.

practical_reading: Deal with today's actual event, good or bad, one at a time, without letting it decide who you are.
misreadings: Not 'feel nothing'; the heart is undefeated, not absent.
Not passive acceptance of harm that can be changed.
cautions: Part of a speech to a bereaved father; gentle as a verse, but avoid implying the reader is 'defeated' if they are grieving.
speaks_to: people swept up by highs and lows
anyone facing a run of unexpected events
not_for: someone enduring abuse or injustice they could act against
the rawest days of loss

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.173.42 (Sanskrit Wikisource, vulgate). BORI 12.168.31 reads 'harṣasthāna-śatāni' (hundreds of occasions for JOY) here; our 'bhayasthāna' (fear) reading is the vulgate one, also found at BORI 12.317.2 and Vana Parva 3.2.15.
attribution_note: The brahmin to Senajit, narrated by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate for our (vulgate) text. The line's 'the wise don't let them ALL in' softens the verse, which says these occasions do not enter the wise at all; acceptable for a reading but note it.
context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; having told him to meet each event with an undefeated heart, he says that every day countless occasions of grief and fear seize the person without discernment but not the wise. The next verse lists who is untouched: the learned, attentive to good teaching, free of envy and self-controlled.

key_terms.sense: occasion for fear (BORI here: harṣasthāna, occasion for elation)

core_teaching: Grief and fear arise from countless daily triggers, but they take hold only where discernment is missing.

commentaries.gist: Grief is rooted in being parted from what one wants, fear in meeting what one does not want; 'enter' means they spread through a person by producing their effects.
Follows the vulgate 'fear' reading and continues that sorrow cannot touch the wise, the self-restrained and the non-envious.
Here the constituted text pairs grief with joy, not fear; the grief-and-fear form is the one used at 12.317.2 and in the Vana Parva.

practical_reading: You cannot stop triggers arriving, but you can learn to recognise them and decline to let each one take over.
misreadings: Not 'anxious people are fools'; it is about cultivated discernment.
Not a claim that wise people never feel anything.
cautions: The verse labels the overwhelmed person 'mūḍha' (deluded); it can shame readers with anxiety disorders or depression.
Original audience is a grieving father.
speaks_to: people learning not to react to every provocation
not_for: clinical anxiety or panic
someone in acute grief who would hear it as 'you are a fool to suffer'
research_note: Edition variant matters for meaning: critical text says grief and JOY. If we cite BORI, change 'fear' accordingly.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.173.47 (Sanskrit Wikisource); BORI 12.168.36. The same couplet recurs in Manki's song (BORI 12.171.51) and at BORI 12.268.6.
attribution_note: The brahmin to Senajit, narrated by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; after saying that whatever desire one gives up fills one with happiness, and that the person who runs after desires is destroyed with them, he states this famous comparison. It is followed by a reflection on past karma and on drawing the senses in like a tortoise.
core_teaching: The quiet that comes when craving ends outweighs every pleasure of earth or heaven.

commentaries.gist: Glosses 'world' as the human world, 'divine' as heavenly, and the end of craving as vairāgya, dispassion.

commentaries.who: Vyasa's bhashya on Yoga Sutra 2.42 (Rama Prasada tr.)
commentaries.gist: Quotes this saying to support the sutra that contentment brings unsurpassed happiness; Vachaspati Mishra links it to Yayati's giving up of desire.
Ganguli renders it as the felicity of the destruction of all desires; BORI shows the line repeated in Manki's song, so it is a refrain of these chapters.

practical_reading: Notice the relief when you stop chasing one more thing; contentment is a positive happiness, not a consolation prize.
misreadings: Not a call to stop meeting basic needs.
Not contempt for ordinary enjoyment; it is a comparison of degree.
cautions: To a grieving reader, calling grief a 'craving' to end would be harsh; keep it to desire and acquisition.
speaks_to: people who achieved goals and still feel empty
not_for: someone in poverty or deprivation
fresh grief, where longing for a person is not craving to be cured

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.173.53 (Sanskrit Wikisource); BORI 12.168.41, which reads 'paritāpārthaṃ sarvaṃ' (the whole of it serves for anguish) where the vulgate has 'paritāpāya nāśe' (for anguish when it is lost). Also BORI 12.268.8.
attribution_note: The brahmin to Senajit, narrated by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate for our vulgate text; the 'when it is lost' clause is absent from BORI.
context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; having urged him to give up even a limb of the body if it is the root of grief, fear or toil, and to draw in the senses like a tortoise, he names the mechanism: whatever is imagined as 'mine' becomes the cause of anguish. He goes on to say that one who neither fears nor is feared, and neither desires nor hates, reaches Brahman.
core_teaching: Pain at loss is in proportion to how much we have made a thing 'mine'; possessiveness is the seed of anguish.

commentaries.gist: Renders the idea of 'meum' as a source of grief and heartburn; his note says the verse appears twice in his text, and the Bombay edition does not repeat it.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource) on the preceding verse
commentaries.gist: On the instruction just before: the root of toil should be dropped even if it is part of one's own body, how much more wealth or wife.
Constituted text says the thing taken as 'mine' wholly becomes a cause of anguish; the same couplet returns in a later Janaka passage.

practical_reading: Hold roles, possessions and even plans a little more loosely; care for them without making your peace depend on keeping them.
misreadings: Not 'don't love people'.
Not a claim that grief is wrong or a sign of selfishness.
cautions: In the story it is said to a father whose son has died; read as 'your grief comes from possessiveness' it would wound a bereaved parent.
speaks_to: fear of losing a job title or status
not_for: bereaved parents or partners
someone who has just lost a home or livelihood

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.173.64 (Sanskrit Wikisource); BORI 12.168.52. A variant of the same line returns in Bodhya's list of teachers (vulgate 12.176.62; BORI star passage 475).
attribution_note: Pingala's own song, quoted by the brahmin to Senajit, inside Bhishma's narration. 'Quoted by Bhishma' is a simplification.
translation_note: Accurate. Our setting adds that she waited 'all night'; the Mahabharata only says the courtesan was left without her lover at the place of meeting. Check the 'all night' detail against the Bhagavata telling (11.8) before using it.
context: Closing his consolation of the grieving King Senajit, the brahmin cites the verses of Pingala, a courtesan who was deprived of her lover at the place of meeting and, in that hard moment, turned her mind to peace. She says she lived long beside the true beloved within without knowing him, that she is now awake, and ends with this verse. Bhishma then says Senajit was persuaded and became glad.

key_terms.sense: freedom from expectation (in modern Hindi 'nirāśā' means despair)

core_teaching: Clinging expectation keeps one awake and suffering; dropping it brings the deepest ease.

commentaries.gist: Treats Pingala's song as allegory: the lover always near is the bliss-giving Self in the heart, and the one-pillared, nine-doored house is the body.
Follows the same reading: she lived beside the Supreme Self without knowing him, is now awake to it, and sleeps happily once free of desire and hope.
The Bhagavata's Pingala ends with the same thought: desire is the greatest misery, its absence the greatest happiness, and having cut off hope for lovers she slept happily.

practical_reading: When your peace hangs on someone else's message, arrival or approval, practise setting the expectation down so you can rest.
misreadings: Not 'hopelessness is happiness'; Hindi readers may hear nirāśā as despair.
Not a judgement on Pingala for her profession; the tradition presents her as a teacher.
cautions: High risk of being heard as endorsing despair by a depressed reader.
Mentions a courtesan and a lover; handle without moralising.
speaks_to: waiting for a call, text or reply
not_for: depression or hopelessness
someone waiting on a medical result or a missing person

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.174.9 (Sanskrit Wikisource, vulgate); Ganguli Santi sec. CLXXV; BORI 12.169.9, where the third line ('amoghā rātrayaḥ...') is only a manuscript addition (star passage 465).
attribution_note: Medhavin to his father, inside Bhishma's narration.
translation_note: Close, but 'falling like arrows' is an interpretive gloss: the verse says the days and nights fall and calls them 'amogha', unfailing. The third line (the unfailing nights keep coming and going) is folded in rather than translated.
context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. The son asks how he can speak so calmly while the world is under attack, surrounded, and struck by unfailing things. The father asks what he means, and the son answers with this verse: death strikes, old age surrounds, and the passing days and nights are what fall. He goes on to say that each night shortens life and that death takes people before their desires are fulfilled.
core_teaching: Every passing day and night shortens life, so one should wake up to mortality instead of postponing what matters.

commentaries.gist: On the son's earlier phrase: the nights are 'unfailing' because each one succeeds in carrying away some of one's life.
Death assails the world, decrepitude surrounds it, and the irresistible things that come and go are the nights that keep lessening human life.
The constituted text frames the whole dialogue with the son's opening worry that a person's life drains away quickly.

practical_reading: Treat today as a real portion of a limited life: pick one thing that truly matters and stop deferring it.
misreadings: Not a reason for panic or morbid dread.
Not a rejection of family life as such; it criticises postponing the highest good.
cautions: Death-centred; can trigger health anxiety or fresh grief.
speaks_to: birthdays and milestones that prompt reflection
not_for: the recently bereaved
people facing terminal illness or with strong death anxiety

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.174.15 (Sanskrit Wikisource); Ganguli sec. CLXXV; BORI 12.169.14ab. The same line recurs at BORI 12.309.72.
attribution_note: Medhavin to his father, narrated by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate. Our line replaces 'death' with 'time', as our_note already says; that softens the verse.
context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. Having said that death snatches people while their minds are elsewhere, the son tells his father to do his good today, because death drags people off with their tasks undone. This verse follows; the next asks who knows whose death will come today, and urges a life of dharma while young.
core_teaching: Because death does not wait for our work to be finished, the work of one's highest good should not be postponed.

commentaries.gist: The verse just before tells the father to do 'what is good' (śreyas) today; the urgency is about the highest good, not about chores.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource) on 174.13
commentaries.gist: Explains the 'flowers' a person is busy picking when death comes as the fruits of desire-driven rites, so the rush the son condemns is the rush after desires.
Renders the line plainly and continues that one should practise virtue in the prime of life since life is transitory.

practical_reading: Do the important thing you keep deferring, the apology, the call, the practice, before the less important urgent things.
misreadings: Not a productivity hack or a case for overwork.
Not 'never rest'.
cautions: Its force rests on death; an anxious reader may hear it as pressure.
speaks_to: people who keep waiting for the 'right time'
not_for: burnout
health anxiety
someone grieving a person who died with things left unsaid (can induce guilt)

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.174.16 (Sanskrit Wikisource); Ganguli sec. CLXXV; BORI 12.169.14ef-15, which reads 'whose camp the army of death will enter today' and 'life has no fixed occasion' (animittam) for 'life is impermanent' (anityam).
attribution_note: Medhavin to his father, narrated by Bhishma.

context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. core_teaching: Since no one knows the day of death, a good life cannot be left for old age; dharma begun young bears fruit here and hereafter.

commentaries.gist: No one knows whether death comes today, so virtue should be practised in the prime of age; it brings fame here and felicity hereafter.
Puts the image more vividly as death's army entering someone's camp today, and gives the life-is-uncertain line as having no fixed cause.
Gives our three-line form with 'anityaṃ khalu jīvitam'; the father's final acceptance of the son's view closes the chapter.

practical_reading: Do not save kindness, honesty or practice for retirement; begin living the life you admire now.
misreadings: Not a claim that young people will die soon.
Not 'fame is the goal'; fame is a by-product.
cautions: Death theme; afterlife promise may feel glib to the bereaved.
speaks_to: young adults deferring values until 'after settling down'
not_for: parents who have lost a child
people with severe health anxiety

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.174.20 (Sanskrit Wikisource); Ganguli sec. CLXXV; BORI 12.169.19, identical.
attribution_note: Medhavin to his father, narrated by Bhishma.
translation_note: 'Attached to his little comforts' misreads 'īhā-sukha-āsakta'. Nilakantha glosses īhā as craving; the phrase means caught up in the pleasure of wanting and striving. Suggest: 'while a person is caught up in the pleasure of planning and striving, death takes him'. The line is fine.
context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. The son describes how death seizes people absorbed in family and acquisition, like a tiger carrying off a sleeping deer. This verse gives the inner voice of such a person, ticking off done, to-do and half-done; the next says death carries off the man attached to field, shop and home before he reaps the fruit of his work.

key_terms.sense: this is done, this is to be done

core_teaching: A life spent in endless to-do lists, enjoying the striving itself, is overtaken by death before it turns to what matters.

commentaries.gist: Defines 'to be done' as what one wishes to do, 'done-not-done' as half-finished, and 'īhā' as craving.
The surrounding lines picture death bearing away the man attached to field, shop and home before he has obtained the fruit of his acts.
Same verse; manuscripts add lines about people thinking 'let this be mine, let that be mine' until death takes them.

practical_reading: Look up from the task list now and then and ask whether the busyness serves anything you care about.
misreadings: Not 'work is pointless'.
Not a judgement on people who must work long hours to survive.
cautions: Death theme; can feed guilt in people already overwhelmed.
speaks_to: people who feel life is passing while they manage tasks
not_for: someone in burnout or overwhelmed by obligations
someone grieving a sudden death

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.174.35 (Sanskrit Wikisource); Ganguli sec. CLXXV. BORI 12.169.33 reads 'nāsti vidyāsamaṃ balam' (no strength like knowledge) for 'nāsti satyasamaṃ tapaḥ'; BORI 12.316.6 has a third form ('no austerity like knowledge').
attribution_note: Medhavin to his father, narrated by Bhishma.
translation_note: Accurate for our vulgate text, which Ganguli also follows.
context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. Near the end, the son resolves to live by truth and non-harm and to offer only inner sacrifices of restraint, study, prayer and meditation, not animal sacrifice. He sums up in this verse, then says he needs no son to save him and asks his father what wealth or wife will help when he dies. Bhishma says the father followed his son's advice.
core_teaching: Knowledge is the truest sight, truthfulness the truest discipline, attachment the deepest sorrow, and letting go the deepest happiness.

commentaries.gist: Gives the fourfold maxim in the vulgate form with truth as the supreme penance, as part of the son's closing resolve.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource) on 174.32
commentaries.gist: The inner sacrifices the son takes up are sense-restraint, reflection on the Upanishads, japa, meditation and service; this is the 'tyāga' he means.
The maxim circulated in several forms; the critical text here praises knowledge as both the best eye and the best strength.

practical_reading: When choosing between holding on and letting go, remember that clinging tends to cost more than it gives.
misreadings: 'Rāga' is attachment, not love or affection for people.
Not a call to abandon family duties; the speaker is a renunciant.
cautions: Comes from a son rejecting the householder path; avoid using it to belittle family life.
speaks_to: people weighing what to let go of
students and seekers wanting a compact rule
someone caught in a draining attachment
not_for: fresh grief, where 'no sorrow like attachment' can sound like blame

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.175.11 (Sanskrit Wikisource); Ganguli Santi sec. CLXXVI (confirmed, not merely inferred); BORI 12.170.11, identical.
attribution_note: Disputed. The text says a brahmin told Bhishma what Shamyaka had sung; Nilakantha (followed by Ganguli) takes the reciter to be someone other than Shamyaka. Safer: 'Verses of Shamyaka, as recited to Bhishma'. Name: Śamyāka in BORI and Wikisource; Śampāka is a variant reading; Ganguli 'Sampaka'.
translation_note: Accurate. Our setting says he 'lost everything'; the text says the reciting brahmin had taken up renunciation and was suffering from a bad wife (Ganguli), poor clothes and hunger. Nothing says he lost a fortune.
context: Yudhishthira asks how happiness and misery come to the rich and the poor. Bhishma recalls verses of Shamyaka, a man who had found peace and freedom, as told to him long ago at Hastinapura by a destitute renunciant brahmin. The verses praise owning nothing: the poor man sleeps and wakes happily, and when poverty and kingship were weighed on a balance, poverty proved heavier. This verse gives the difference; the next says neither fire, death nor robbers can touch the one who has let go of wealth, and then describes the arrogance that wealth breeds.

key_terms.sense: as if in the jaws of death

core_teaching: Wealth brings constant anxiety about loss, which the person who owns nothing is free of.

commentaries.gist: Someone else told Bhishma what Shamyaka sang; the speaker was destitute, lacking food and clothing; the poor man's path is free of enemies and hard to reach for those full of desire.
Translates the weighing of poverty against sovereignty and the rich man's agitation; his note says the commentator's view of the speaker strains the grammar of the last verse.
Same text; the chapter ends with Bhishma saying that for this reason he holds renunciation to be the highest.

practical_reading: Notice how much worry each new possession or commitment brings, and weigh that cost before acquiring more.
misreadings: Not a case against earning a living or supporting a family.
Not a romantic view of real poverty.
cautions: Can sound glib to readers in financial hardship.
speaks_to: anxiety about protecting wealth or status
not_for: someone struggling to pay for basics
someone who has just lost their savings or job

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.175.22 (Sanskrit Wikisource); Ganguli sec. CLXXVI; BORI 12.170.22, which ends 'sukhī bhava' (be happy) instead of 'sukhī bhavet' (one becomes happy).
attribution_note: As for 12.175.11: verses of Shamyaka, recited to Bhishma by a brahmin whom Nilakantha takes to be someone else.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Yudhishthira asks how happiness and misery come to the rich and the poor. Bhishma recalls verses of Shamyaka, a man who had found peace and freedom, as told to him long ago at Hastinapura by a destitute renunciant brahmin. After showing how wealth breeds pride, waste and finally theft and punishment, the verses advise treating these sorrows with understanding as a medicine, knowing the way of the world. This is the closing verse; Bhishma then says this is why he regards renunciation as foremost.
core_teaching: Happiness, the highest good and fearless rest all come only through letting go.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource) on 175.21
commentaries.gist: The 'medicine' the verses prescribe for great sorrows is a remedy applied through understanding.
Renders the threefold 'without renunciation' and Bhishma's conclusion that renunciation is foremost.
Places the verse after the advice to understand the world's mixture of the stable and unstable, and ends with Bhishma's verdict for renunciation.

practical_reading: Find one thing you are gripping, a grudge, a plan, a possession, and loosen your hold on it so you can rest.
misreadings: Not 'abandon your family or responsibilities'.
Not 'give up on life'.
cautions: 'Let go of everything' must never be read as giving up on life; avoid for any reader who may be at risk of self-harm.
Literal total renunciation is the original sense.
speaks_to: people unable to sleep from worry over possessions or plans
not_for: anyone expressing hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm
someone in acute grief

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.176.43 (Sanskrit Wikisource); Ganguli Santi sec. CLXXVII; BORI 12.171.43, which reads 'kṣamiṣye 'kṣamamāṇānām' (I will bear with the unforbearing) for 'kṣipamāṇānām' (those who revile me).
attribution_note: Manki, addressing Desire (Kāma), narrated by Bhishma. Listener 'Desire (himself)' is fine.
translation_note: Accurate for our vulgate text. Prasang summary: the oxen were killed when a camel carried them off, which is fine to call an accident.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a man who keeps striving and fails to gain wealth can be happy. Bhishma tells of Manki, who after repeated failures spent his last money on a pair of young bullocks; while being trained they ran at a resting camel, which rose and bolted with both dangling from its neck to their death. Manki first blames fate, then turns on Desire itself: he knows its root is mental intention and will no longer feed it. Casting Desire off, he vows forbearance and gentle speech, then says he will live content on whatever comes and has entered Brahman like a man plunging into a cool lake in summer.

key_terms.sense: I will not harm when harmed

core_teaching: One freed from desire answers insult with patience, harm with non-harm, and hostility with kind words.

commentaries.gist: 'Kṣipamāṇa' means those who scorn or revile; in the next verse 'content' means living on what comes without feeding Desire.

Renders the vow of forgiveness, non-retaliation and agreeable speech as the fruit of Manki's renunciation, followed by his list of new virtues: tranquillity, truth, self-restraint, forgiveness and compassion.
Constituted text puts the vow right after Manki casts off Desire, and frames the whole song as born of nirveda, disenchantment.

practical_reading: When someone is harsh, choose not to retaliate and reply in a calm, kind tone, while still protecting yourself.
misreadings: Not 'stay in an abusive situation'.
Not 'never set boundaries or seek justice'.
cautions: A renunciant's vow; applied to a victim of abuse it could be harmful.
speaks_to: someone wanting to stop escalating conflicts
not_for: victims of abuse, harassment or bullying
someone seeking justice for a serious wrong

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.176.56 (Sanskrit Wikisource); Ganguli Santi sec. CLXXVIII (opening); BORI 12.171.56, which reads 'anantaṃ bata' (ah, endless) for 'anantam iva' (as if endless). Also at BORI 12.17.18 (Yudhishthira quoting Janaka) and 12.268.4.
attribution_note: King Janaka of Videha, quoted by Bhishma to Yudhishthira. Our listener field is blank; fill as 'quoted to Yudhishthira'.
translation_note: Accurate for 'iva'.
context: Bhishma ends the story of Manki and adds, on the same theme, the verse sung by Janaka, king of Videha, who had reached peace. He then moves to the sage Bodhya and his six teachers. The saying is very widely shared: Buddhist literature gives the same words to King Janaka in the Mahajanaka Jataka, where his queen sets fires around Mithila to call him back from renunciation.

key_terms.sense: my wealth is as if endless

core_teaching: One who owns nothing inwardly has a wealth that cannot be lost; even if his city burns, nothing of his is burned.

commentaries.gist: Renders it as a paradox, unlimited wealth and yet nothing owned, so the burning of Mithila is no loss to him.

In the Buddhist Mahajanaka Jataka the renouncing king answers his queen's fires with this verse; Appleton notes it recurs across Hindu, Buddhist and Jain literature, exploring duty versus renunciation.
Constituted text has the exclamatory 'ah, endless'; the Shanti Parva quotes the verse in three places.

practical_reading: Hold your role and belongings as a steward, not an owner, so a loss does not destroy your sense of self.
misreadings: Not 'don't care for anything'; care without clutching.
Not a model for a leader ignoring a real disaster.
cautions: The burning-city image would hurt someone who has lost a home to fire or disaster.
speaks_to: fear of losing a position or possessions
leaders who feel their identity depends on their role
not_for: survivors of fire, flood or displacement
someone who has just been robbed or evicted

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.176.63 (Sanskrit Wikisource, inside a passage the edition brackets as an addition); Ganguli sec. CLXXVIII. Not in the BORI constituted text: BORI star passage 475, line 3, inserted after 12.171.61.
attribution_note: Speaker error. Bodhya only lists his six teachers; this gloss on the osprey is introduced with 'Bhishma said' in Wikisource, in BORI's star passage and in Ganguli ('Bhishma continued'). Correct to Bhishma, to Yudhishthira. Listener: Yayati in the vulgate, Nahusha in BORI.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Bhishma says the old saying of the sage Bodhya also concerns disenchantment. A king (in the vulgate the son of Nahusha, Yayati; in BORI Nahusha himself) asks the calm Bodhya what understanding gives him peace. Bodhya says he teaches no one, but names his six teachers: Pingala, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden. The verses explaining each teacher follow under the heading 'Bhishma said' in both the vulgate and the manuscripts BORI records. After Pingala, the osprey: carrying meat it is set upon by birds that have none, and by dropping the meat it is left in peace. Next come the snake that lives in another's hole, the bee, the absorbed arrow-maker and the maiden's single bangle.
core_teaching: What we grab makes us a target; letting go of the prize ends the conflict and brings peace.

commentaries.gist: Gives the six teachers and, under 'Bhishma continued', the osprey set on by birds without meat and finding happiness once it gives the meat up.
Explains the 'sāraṅga' in the list as a bee and its 'following' as imitation; the passage containing this verse is bracketed in the Wikisource text as an addition.
The Bhagavata's brahmin teacher uses the same image: stronger hawks without prey attack the one holding meat, and it finds happiness by dropping it.

practical_reading: If holding on to something is drawing constant conflict, a promotion fight, a family property, an argument, consider whether dropping it buys you peace.
misreadings: Not 'always give in to bullies'.
Not 'never own anything'.
cautions: Could be read as advice to surrender rights to aggressors; keep it to voluntary letting go.
speaks_to: rivalry over a prize or position
not_for: someone being coerced or robbed
someone fighting for something they need to live
research_note: Prasang summary lists 'the deer' among the teachers; Nilakantha and Ganguli take sāraṅga as the bee. our_note calls the Bhagavata parallel the 'Avadhuta Gita'; the parallel is the Bhagavata's brahmin and his teachers (Book 11, ch. 7-9), better named that way.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.176.67 (Sanskrit Wikisource, bracketed addition); Ganguli sec. CLXXVIII. Not in the BORI constituted text: BORI star passage 475, line 9, which reads 'iṣāv āhitamānasaḥ' (mind fixed on the arrow).
attribution_note: Same speaker error as 12.176.63: the gloss is spoken by Bhishma, not Bodhya. Listener Yayati (vulgate) or Nahusha (BORI).
translation_note: Accurate. Our Sanskrit has a typo copied from Wikisource: 'कश्चिदिपावासक्तमानसः' should be 'कश्चिदिषावासक्तमानसः' (iṣau āsakta-mānasaḥ, mind attached to the arrow).
context: Bhishma says the old saying of the sage Bodhya also concerns disenchantment. A king (in the vulgate the son of Nahusha, Yayati; in BORI Nahusha himself) asks the calm Bodhya what understanding gives him peace. Bodhya says he teaches no one, but names his six teachers: Pingala, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden. The verses explaining each teacher follow under the heading 'Bhishma said' in both the vulgate and the manuscripts BORI records. After Pingala, the osprey, the snake and the bee, the arrow-maker: a man so intent on his arrow that he did not notice the king passing beside him. Last is the maiden whose single shell bangle makes no noise, a lesson in solitude.
core_teaching: Total absorption of the mind in one task makes it oblivious to every distraction, even a passing king; this is the model of concentration.

commentaries.gist: The maker of shafts was so attentive to his work that the king passing by went unnoticed; it stands among Bodhya's lessons in detachment.
Uses the same arrow-maker as an image of a mind fixed so completely on the Absolute that it no longer registers inside or outside.
The constituted text only names the six teachers; the explanations, including this one, survive as a manuscript addition headed 'Bhishma said'.

practical_reading: Give one task your undivided attention for a stretch, phone away, and let lesser things pass by unnoticed.
misreadings: Not 'ignore people or authority'.
Not a celebration of workaholism; the point is the gathered mind.
cautions: Low risk. Avoid framing it as a judgement on readers who struggle with attention.
not_for: someone neglecting people around them through over-absorption in work
research_note: Prasang summary: 'the deer' should be 'the bee'; and the six teachers' explanations are Bhishma's in all texts checked.
